title: Detroit Lions stock report: Risers, fallers at every position vs. Bengals
summary: The Detroit Lions’ first preseason game of the 2026 season is in the books, and it’s time to check in on the players who helped or hurt their stock against the Cincinnati Bengals. Attendance The Lions rested 32 players (including 18 starters) along with another three on injury lists (PUP/NFI). Let’s take a quick look at the […]
full_text: Aug 13, 2026; Cincinnati, Ohio, USA; Detroit Lions running back Jacob Saylors (25) runs with the ball against the Cincinnati Bengals in the first half at Paycor Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Katie Stratman-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Detroit Lions’ first preseason game of the 2026 season is in the books, and it’s time to check in on the players who helped or hurt their stock against the Cincinnati Bengals. Attendance The Lions rested 32 players (including 18 starters) along with another three on injury lists (PUP/NFI). Let’s take a quick look at the roster with our game-day depth chart , noting that the players without a position color did not play in this game. Additionally, if a player’s name is written in red, they came into the game injured; if they were injured during the game, their name is boxed in black. Quarterback Stock up: Luke Altmyer Stock neutral: Josh Dobbs Did not play: Jared Goff Stats: If you didn’t watch the game and only looked at the box score, you’d be pretty underwhelmed by the Lions quarterbacks’ performances, but of course, stats don’t tell the whole story. Altmyer got the start and played roughly two-thirds of offensive snaps , and while his numbers show below-average plays, the moment never looked too big for him. Yes, he made mistakes you’d expect from an undrafted rookie, but he was efficient from a communications standpoint, stayed poised in the pocket, and trusted his teammates—even after being let down on previous plays. You can also give Altmyer a bit of grace on his turnovers, as the first interception bounced off Issac TeSlaa to a defender, the second pick was a result of him forcing the issue late in the game trying to make a play (though he did sail the ball too high), and the fumble was due to a wet ball on the handoff. Those are errors he’ll need to overcome if he wants to make the 53-man roster, but as coach Dan Campbell pointed out after the game, they also present learning opportunities. “I thought Luke did a really good job for a young guy,” Campbell said. “I’ve got to be careful; I don’t want to give him too much sugar and tea time. But what you see in practice—the composure, not too big for him, the accuracy, those deep balls—he’s got a touch about them. I felt like he showed up. The mistakes that he did make, they’re great. You have to have those to learn from, in any position, but especially his. I felt like it was a good debut for him.” Running back Stock up: Jacob Saylors, Raheem Blackshear Stock down: Kye Robichaux Did not play: Jahmyr Gibbs Injury: Isiah Pacheco (MCL sprain), Sione Vaki (nose/eye), Jabari Small (undisclosed) In the battle for RB4, Saylors took a massive step forward on Thursday night, leading the team in rushing attempts, yards, average yards per carry, receptions, and receiving yards. He got involved in the offense in a variety of ways, was decisive as a runner, looked shifty in his movement, and produced results on different routes. A very complete game overall. “He was probably our most potent player on offense, Campbell said of Saylors post-game. ”He made a lot of plays for us. He’s a steady workhorse.” Blackshear showed some promise that is worth investing in—including a sweet 24-yard run—while Robichaux continues to look strong as a downhill runner, but doesn’t offer much beyond that. Wide receiver Stock up: Dominic Lovett, Tay Martin, Tarik Black Stock neutral: Greg Dortch, Cedrick Wilson, Lucky Jackson Stock down: Isaac TeSlaa, Tom Kennedy, Malik Cunningham Did not play: Amon-Ra St. Brown, Jameson Williams Injury: None While Campbell continues to hype the receiving room, I feel like I am continually left wanting more. Maybe I’m spoiled by getting to watch Amon-Ra and Jamo so often, but there’s room to grow for everyone who played on Thursday night. TeSlaa’s rough preseason continued against the Bengals. He was targeted three times, failed to catch a pass, and one bounced off his helmet, deflected in the air, and led to an interception. Campbell insists that he isn’t worried and that TeSlaa will “be fine,” but he needs to start stacking wins soon if he hopes to be involved in the offense early in the season. “I remember what those days were like. You want everything to come early; you can come into your second season and place a lot of pressure on yourself. You want to be great. Just stay the course,” Campbell empathized after the game. In the race for WR5, Dominic Lovett and Tay Martin got the first (and most) opportunities on the field amongst the reserves, but it was Lovett who took a bigger step forward. While Martin hauled in his only target for 14 yards, Lovett was targeted eight times (catching three for 28 yards), illustrating his ability to get open quickly in his routes. Veterans Tom Kennedy and Malik Cunningham each had one reception, but both look like they may be falling behind in the competition for a roster spot. Tight end Stock up: Jackson Meeks Stock neutral: Tyler Conklin Stock down: Thomas Gordon, Zach Horton Did not play: Sam LaPorta, Brock Wright Conklin and Meeks got the start, with the veteran securing two receptions and the WR-convert producing a 17-yard reception, picking up 16 of those yards after the catch. Meeks was believed to be in a competition with Thomas for a TE4 role, but Meeks was clearly favored by the coaching staff in this game and looks to be ahead. Offensive line Stock up: RT Blake Miller*, LT Larry Borom Stock neutral: LG Christian Mahogany, C Michael Niese, LG Melvin Priestly*, RG Mason Miller, RT Colby Sorsdal Stock down: C Seth McLaughlin, RG/LT Miles Frazier Did not play: Penei Sewell, Tate Ratledge Injury: Cade Mays (wrist), Juice Scruggs (soft tissue), Ben Bartch (undisclosed), Devin Cochran (undisclosed), Giovanni Manu (NFI) Offensive line is the hardest group to evaluate during a live game—which is why the second unit almost all landed in the “neutral” group—but the main takeaway I had from watching this game was that most of the Bengals’ pressure was generated up the middle and not on the edges, a good sign for Miller and Borom. . @Lions @BlakeMillerOT played the entire first half…Looked like he belongs …Working v @aidanhutch97 everyday can speed up the learning phase… #onepride #BaldysBreakdowns pic.twitter.com/tyoweCY10h — Brian Baldinger (@BaldyNFL) August 14, 2026 Frazier landed in my stock down section because of three holding penalties in the first half while playing right guard, but I considered moving him out of this section after he looked solid at left tackle in the second half. McLaughlin also landed in the down section after an up-and-down performance and what I saw as a few communication issues, but he flashed some good reps that point to potential improvement over the next two weeks/games. It also didn’t help that Niese, his depth competition, looked solid with the second team. Defensive tackle Stock up: Skyler Gill-Howard*, Chris Smith Stock neutral: Levi Onwuzurike, Mekhi Wingo ( injured ) Stock down: Myles Adams, Ben Stille, Tyre West* Did not play: Alim McNeill, Tyleik Williams Injury: One of the big winners of the night was rookie Gill-Howard, who continues to ascend up the depth chart. While he is currently repping third or fourth at the 3-technique, he is getting mixed in with the second team and making plays when given the opportunity. On the night, he had two of the defense’s top-5 plays, both drive-ending plays: generating a pressure on fourth down that resulted in intentional grounding, and running down QB Josh Johnson on third down to stop him short of the sticks. He also added in a pressure/QB hit for good measure. “Watching Skyler (Gill-Howard) get to the quarterback there, it was a critical fourth down to get the offense the ball. That takes a tremendous amount of effort, but that’s what is expected; that was awesome,” Campbell said post-game. Fellow rookie, West, saw just four snaps in the game and has a lot of work to do to get in reach of a roster spot. Defensive end…

full_text: Aug 13, 2026; Cincinnati, Ohio, USA; Members of the Detroit Lions huddle before a play in the first half against the Cincinnati Bengals at Paycor Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Katie Stratman-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect As always in the preseason, there were plenty of ups and downs during the Detroit Lions’ 16-14 loss to the Cincinnati Bengals in what was the first ot three scheduled exhibition games. On the offensive side of the ball, rookie quarterback Luke Altmyer looked calm and cool operating the Lions’ offense, while it was a night to forget for second-year wide receiver Isaac TeSlaa. On one occasion, an Altmyer pass bounced off TeSlaa’s facemask, sending the ball straight into the air and eventually, directly into the hands of the defense. In general, it’s been a tough training camp for the Hudsonville native, and I would expect the coaching staff to continue to load him up with reps as the preseason marches on. On the other side of the ball, defensive end Ahmed Hassanein’s stock continues to rise after he made a handful of splash plays, including a first-series sack on Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow and a sack-fumble later in the game. There were plenty of other takeaways from the game, leading us to today’s question of the day: What was your biggest takeaway from the Lions’ first preseason game? My answer: I am going with Hassanein looking like a bona fide NFL player. More than that, if he is able to stack great days like the one he had against the Bengals, he is going to firmly be part of the rotation along the defensive line. Coming out of Boise State, nobody questioned Hassanein’s potential if he landed in the right situation, and now we are beginning to understand why. Simply put, the young man plays like his hair is on fire. And while that sometimes needs to be reined in, as Lions coach Dan Campbell said, it’s better to have that problem than the other way around. I still need to watch the tape from the first game, but I really liked what I saw from the broadcast angle, and I am certain Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard did, too. What about you? What was your biggest takeaway from the Lions’ first preseason game against the Bengals? Let us know in the comments below.

title: What Lions vs. Bengals snap counts tell us about Detroit’s roster
summary: Snap counts—and more importantly, order of lineups—in the preseason can be very telling as to where each player currently stands in the depth chart. So we took a closer look at the participation of individual Detroit Lions players in their preseason opener against the Cincinnati Bengals. Here’s what we found. Quarterbacks: Luke Altmyer nearly got […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OH - AUGUST 13: Quarterback Luke Altmyer #2 of the Detroit Lions runs for a 2-point conversion in a preseason game between the Detroit Lions and the Cincinnati Bengals on August 13, 2026, at Paycor Stadium in Cincinnati, OH. (Photo by Jeff Moreland/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Snap counts—and more importantly, order of lineups—in the preseason can be very telling as to where each player currently stands in the depth chart. So we took a closer look at the participation of individual Detroit Lions players in their preseason opener against the Cincinnati Bengals. Here’s what we found. Quarterbacks: Luke Altmyer: 44 snaps (67%) Josh Dobbs: 22 (33%) Jared Goff: DNP Luke Altmyer nearly got the entire game, but Josh Dobbs stepped in during the second quarter. At first, it appeared the Lions may have benched Altmyer after he fumbled, but coach Dan Campbell clarified after the game that the plan was always to give Dobbs some reps with the “starting” offensive line. With a strong performance from Altmyer, it’ll be fascinating to see if he can win the backup job over Dobbs, but the fact that Detroit wanted to get the veteran quarterback some early reps in the first half suggests to me that they want to get him ready to be the primary backup. Running backs: Jacob Saylors: 29 (44%) — 3 special teams snaps (12%) Kye Robichaux: 21 (32%) — 8 (32%) Raheem Blackshear: 16 (24%) — 7 (28%) Jahmyr Gibbs: DNP Isiah Pacheco: DNP (injury) Sione Vaki: DNP (injury) Jabari Small: DNP (injury) Saylors got the start and played extremely well, as he continues to make a strong case to be the team’s RB4 for the second straight season. Unfortunately, his main competition—Jabari Small—is still being held out with what is likely a knee injury. Raheem Blackshear, who was only added recently, got some praise from Campbell after the game, but he’ll need to stack more performances to move his way into the conversation. And while Sione Vaki didn’t play as he continues to rest following a nose and eye injury, his roster spot is pretty safe after Campbell essentially locked him in as RB3 on Thursday night while praising Saylors. “We know those two backs (Jahmyr Gibbs and Isiah Pacheco) at the top and we know what (Sione) Vaki is, he’s one of the best special teams players in the league. So, if that fourth running back is going to make it, he’s going to need to help on special teams.” Wide receivers: Dominic Lovett: 32 (48%) — 7 (28%) Tay Martin: 30 (45%) — 7 (28%) Tom Kennedy: 25 (38%) Lucky Jackson: 17 (26%) — 7 (28%) Isaac TeSlaa: 17 (26%) Tarik Black: 16 (24%) — 7 (28%) Cedrick Wilson: 15 (23%) Malik Cunningham: 14 (21%) — 8 (32%) Greg Dortch: 7 (11%) — 1 (4%) Amon-Ra St. Brown: DNP Jameson Williams: DNP Isaac TeSlaa got plenty of reps, with the Lions hoping the second-year receiver could shake his slow start to training camp. Unfortunately, that didn’t happen. Detroit’s WR4, Greg Dortch, barely played any, further cementing his spot on the roster. Meanwhile, the WR5 battle is continuing to heat up. Dominic Lovett’s play was up and down, with him making a few big catches, a couple drops, and a muffed punt (that he recovered). Meanwhile, Tay Martin had a nice grab, and Tarik Black had Detroit’s only touchdown—and a nice catch called by an iffy pass interference. It was a quiet day for Tom Kennedy, and his lack of any special teams reps could certainly be notable. Tight ends: Tyler Gordon: 25 (38%) — 7 (28%) Jackson Meeks: 24 (36%) — 9 (36%) Zach Horton: 22 (33%) — 13 (52%) Tyler Conklin: 17 (26%) Sam LaPorta: DNP Brock Wright: DNP Tyler Conklin got his feet wet early in the game, which is a good sign for his injury progress. He continues to be the heavy favorite for the TE3 job. Meanwhile, Jackson Meeks got the earliest play of the reserves, suggesting he’s higher on the depth chart than Tyler Gordon and Zach Horton, who played deep into the game. Offensive tackle: Miles Frazier: 66 (100%) Blake Miller: 39 (59%) — 3 (12%) Larry Borom: 39 (59%) — 3 (12%) Colby Sorsdal: 27 (41%) — 3 (12%) Penei Sewell: DNP Devin Cochran: DNP (presumably injury) Guard/center: Seth McLaughlin: 39 (59%) — 3 (12%) Christian Mahogany: 39 (59%) — 3 (12%) Mason Miller: 27 (41%) — 3 (12%) Michael Niese: 27 (41%) Melvin Priestly: 27 (41%) Tate Ratledge: DNP Ben Bartch: DNP (injury?) Juice Scruggs: DNP (injury) Cade Mays: DNP (injury) The first-team offensive line looked like this: LT: Larry Borom LG: Christian Mahogany C: Seth McLaughlin RG: Miles Frazier RT: Blake Miller And the second-team offensive line looked like this: LT: Miles Frazier LG: Melvin Priestly C: Michael Niese RG: Mason Miller RT: Colby Sorsdal And they didn’t stray from those two lineups the entire game. McLaughlin’s Lions debut was very hot and cold, while it was a tough night for Miles Frazier, who was flagged for holding three times. First-round pick Blake Miller got plenty of work in the game, and Campbell was optimistic about his debut, although he ceded his full judgment until he got a look at the replay of the game. “I felt like my eyes were never on he or Larry (Borom) and that’s a positive,” Campbell said. “That’s a pretty good sign that they’re handling their business. We didn’t have any issues on the perimeter.” Defensive end: Anthony Lucas: 50 (71%) Eric O’Neill: 38 (54%) Ahmed Hassanein: 29 (41%) — 9 (36%) Tyler Lacy: 13 (19%) Aidan Hutchinson: DNP DJ Wonnum: DNP Payton Turner: DNP (injury) Derrick Moore: DNP (Injury) Lucas played both early and late in the game, so it’s hard to get a read on his status with the team, but the biggest story from this group is Hassanein . He tallied a sack on his very first snap, and followed it up with another in the second half, as he moves closer and closer to a roster lock. Eric O’Neill was also forced to play a ton and started making an impact late in the game. Meanwhile, presumed starter Tyler Lacy only played a little early in the game, as the Lions were shorthanded at this position. Wingo came in shortly thereafter and suffered an injury that may place him in concussion protocol . That gave way to more opportunities for Gill-Howard, and he ran with it. He produced a few big plays, including a pressure that led to a fourth-down intentional grounding call and an impressive chase down of quarterback Josh Johnson to force a third-down stop. Linebacker: Erick Hunter: 43 (61%) — 12 (48%) Joe Bachie: 27 (39%) — 14 (56%) Trevor Nowaske: 27 (39%) Troy Reeder: 22 (31%) — 10 (40%) Devin White: 22 (31%) Amen Ogbongbemiga: 13 (19%) — 9 (36%) Jack Campbell: DNP Derrick Barnes: DNP Malcolm Rodriguez: DNP (injured) Damone Clark: DNP (injured) Jimmy Rolder: DNP (injured) White and Nowaske got the start, but what I find most interesting here is that Nowaske didn’t get a single special teams rep. Undrafted rookie Erick Hunter got a ton of playing time during the game and flashed both his strengths and weaknesses. title: 5 Detroit Lions players who helped their roster chances in Bengals preseason game
summary: The first preseason game of the Detroit Lions’ 2026 season is in the books, albeit with a losing score of 16-14 in favor of the Cincinnati Bengals. However, wins and losses are secondary facts of the preseason. What truly matters is using these live snaps as learning tools for both players and coaches alike. For […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - AUGUST 13: Jacob Saylors #25 of the Detroit Lions is chased by Daijahn Anthony #33 of the Cincinnati Bengals during the second quarter of a preseason game at Paycor Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images The first preseason game of the Detroit Lions’ 2026 season is in the books, albeit with a losing score of 16-14 in favor of the Cincinnati Bengals. However, wins and losses are secondary facts of the preseason. What truly matters is using these live snaps as learning tools for both players and coaches alike. For players, especially rookies, these can be their first reps all year against opposing professional players. For coaches, playing against an unpredictable opponent is the best opportunity to examine how your roster shapes up. This can be a crucial step in deciding which way the roster battles end. Let us look at five roster bubble players that stood out against the Bengals: Ahmed Hassanein, DE Hassanein was without question the most impactful player on either side of the ball for the Lions. He was wreaking havoc up front from the get-go, regardless of whether he was facing Cincinnati’s starters or reserves. On his very first snap, he sacked Joe Burrow on a stunt where he demonstrated some solid closing speed— and some psychic ability . He would remain active throughout the game, recording a fair number of pressures and quarterback hits. Midway through the third quarter, Hassanein notched himself a strip sack of Josh Johnson. If Hassanein was on the roster bubble entering Thursday, I think he is officially as close to a roster lock as you can get. Unless Payton Turner plays at an otherworldly level upon his return from injury, Hassanein looks like the clear-cut fifth edge option behind Aidan Hutchinson, DJ Wonnum, Derrick Moore, and Tyler Lacy—and if he has a few more games like these, he could legitimately push Lacy for the starting big end spot. Jacob Saylors, RB Although Saylors had a leg-up on the potential RB4 position, there was still an earnest competition between him and Jabari Small. With Small held out (presumably) due to injury, it was Saylors’ time to shine, and shine he did. He turned eight carries into 55 yards, while also tying for the team lead in receiving with three catches for 28 yards. His performance checked a lot of boxes: he looked fast, he looked strong, he looked agile, he looked reliable, and, best of all, his gloveless aesthetic was impeccable . This battle is far from over, and I expect Small to get a fair look, but Saylors has landed the early blow in this tight training camp battle. Nick Whiteside, CB You have got to love when a player backs up their training camp hype. Whiteside was by far the biggest winner of training camp thus far , but turning good practices into good games does not always come easy. Thankfully, Whiteside had a solid game against the Bengals. The stat sheet is not eye-popping, with just a single tackle to his name, but he was challenging the Cincinnati quarterbacks with sticky coverage throughout the game. On his best play of the game, he recovered from an early stumble and made a beautiful leaping pass breakup that would have otherwise gone for a massive gain. While D.J. Reed and Rock Ya-Sin seem locked into the starting outside cornerback roles, Whiteside is making a strong case to be the top reserve, especially with Ennis Rakestraw yet again leaving a football game due to injury. Even if Rakestraw returns from what is initially believed to be a non-serious injury , I think Whiteside has jumped him on the depth chart until proven otherwise. Eric O’Neill, DE The Lions had a fair number of undrafted rookies with hype entering this preseason game, but O’Neill had largely flown under the radar in camp. That was not the case on Thursday night as he was one of the more impactful players along the front seven. He recorded at least three pressures (based on observations; the stats are still pending), including a quarterback hit on Burrow and a great tackle for loss late in the fourth quarter. O’Neill was seeing snaps early in the first quarter against Bengals starters and played into the fourth quarter, and he rarely looked gassed. His early snaps are likely a byproduct of Hutchinson, Wonnum, Lacy, and Turner being held out, but it was nonetheless a positive sight for the undrafted rookie to get so many snaps and look good while doing so. He is still off the roster bubble, but he is worth watching going forward. Skyler Gill-Howard, DT Despite the team recording just two sacks, the fact that I am giving so many defensive linemen positive remarks shows how well they were playing against the Bengals. Gill-Howard did not record a sack, but there were two specific plays that highlighted why the Lions see potential in him. Late in the second quarter, Gill-Howard pressured Johnson thanks to a well-executed swim move, forcing a throwaway and an intentional grounding call. Jalen Rivers beaten badly pic.twitter.com/1XMRD2S0qt — Goodberry (@JoeGoodberry) August 14, 2026 Late in the fourth quarter, Gill-Howard was again hot on the heels of Johnson, this time chasing down the aged-but-still-elusive quarterback for a mere 1-yard gain, forcing a field goal attempt. Gill-Howard’s ability to move at 280 pounds is quite impressive, and it was nice to see him look like an impactful player from the start. As a sixth-round pick, his roster spot is not guaranteed, but I would be very surprised if he did not make this roster.

title: Ahmed Hassanein called his shot, sacking Joe Burrow on 1st snap
summary: Detroit Lions defensive end Ahmed Hassanein had to compose himself. He had just accomplished a lifelong dream of his and was breaking down and crying. But it was third down, and the second-team Lions defense was trying to get an early stop going against the Cincinnati Bengals. Let’s back up. Before Thursday night’s preseason opener, […]
full_text: Detroit Lions defensive lineman Ahmed Hassanein (61) speaks after practice during rookie mini camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Friday, May 9, 2025. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Detroit Lions defensive end Ahmed Hassanein had to compose himself. He had just accomplished a lifelong dream of his and was breaking down and crying. But it was third down, and the second-team Lions defense was trying to get an early stop going against the Cincinnati Bengals. Let’s back up. Before Thursday night’s preseason opener, Hassanein was getting in one last cram session. He was watching tape, preparing for his first football action since last preseason, and, more importantly, he was manifesting. He knew he was going up against one of the best quarterbacks in football in Joe Burrow. All he wanted was to sack Burrow. So he spent all day telling everyone—coach Dan Campbell, his wife—that he was going to do just that. “I truly, truly prayed about it and I manifested it,” Hassanein said after the game. “And I said, I’m going to sack him before the game. And coach Campbell said the same thing. I just kept telling my wife, ‘I’m going to sack Joe Burrow, I’m going to get him.’ I just kept talking to God about it.” Then, on the Lions’ fourth defensive snap of the game, Hassanein substituted in for his first snap of preseason football. You already know what happened next: Ahmed got 'em! pic.twitter.com/qLYfqIXgVr — Detroit Lions (@Lions) August 13, 2026 After initially getting stymied, Hassanein made an inside move, tapped into his relentless motor, and took down Burrow. And when it happened, the emotions overtook the moment. “I cried. I didn’t know what to do. I literally broke down,” Hassanein said. “But I had to go back on defense.” Hassanein has been one of the biggest stories of Lions training camp. Coming into 2026, he was still considered a very raw player with a great story and an even greater football character, but expectations remained relatively low. However, he’s been one of the most explosive and consistent playmakers on defense since camp opened up. And by translating that promise on game days, he’s starting to earn the trust of his coaches. “I don’t feel like I’m surprised,” coach Dan Campbell said Thursday night. “I felt like they came out and made plays. Just the way Ahmed played, the things he’s able to do, you feel like it would translate, certainly with this preseason. It was good to see; it was maximum effort.” Hassanein wasn’t done. In the third quarter, he bent around the Bengals left tackle and swatted the ball out of Josh Johnson’s hands for a third-down strip sack. That, too, was the result of his relentless preparation. “We always credit (defensive line) coach Kacy Rodgers. When you get a rush, you have to reach for it,” Hassanein said. “When the ball is going to be there—we call it a tomahawk on air—you just reach, reach, reach, reach. And then the ball is going to be there.” Hassanein’s story has now become much more than just a feel-good narrative to take you through the offseason. He has a real chance to not only make the roster, but to make an impact on defense this year. But the second-year defensive lineman is not thinking too far down the road. “There is so much work to be done, and I have a feeling I’m going to get so much better because I’m going to keep working,” Hassanein said. “I’m going to keep stacking, and I’m just going to not look too far ahead and too far behind.”

title: Here’s who played for the Packers’ 1st- and 2nd-team units in the preseason opener
summary: The Green Bay Packers’ snap counts from their preseason opener against the Pittsburgh Steelers dropped yesterday, but they don’t tell you very much. When players like cornerback Jaylin Simpson are leading the team in total snaps, it doesn’t really paint a clear picture of who is getting in the mix with the Packers’ first- and […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - AUGUST 18: Jonathan Ford #99 of the Green Bay Packers walks along the field during an NFL football game against the Denver Broncos at Empower Field at Mile High on August 18, 2024 in Denver, CO. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers’ snap counts from their preseason opener against the Pittsburgh Steelers dropped yesterday, but they don’t tell you very much. When players like cornerback Jaylin Simpson are leading the team in total snaps, it doesn’t really paint a clear picture of who is getting in the mix with the Packers’ first- and second-team units. So as a gift to you, I have charted all of the Packers’ first- and second-team snaps against the Steelers, on both the offensive and defensive sides of the ball. This gives us a better look at what Green Bay’s depth chart looks like right now, compared to raw snap counts. I hope you enjoy (and I’ll be doing this moving forward in the preseason, too). I’ also added some notes when I thought they were relevant. Packers 1st Team Offense Quarterback Jordan Love: 9 snaps Running Back MarShawn Lloyd: 9 snaps Reminder: Josh Jacobs (groin) and Chris Brooks (hamstring) were both held out of the game with injuries. Receiver Matthew Golden: 9 snaps Christian Watson: 8 snaps Jayden Reed: 7 snaps Savion Williams: 1 snap As expected, Jayden Reed only got on the field in three-receiver sets, as he’s been used almost exclusively as a slot receiver in his time with Green Bay . That doesn’t seem to be changing in 2026. Savion Williams got in for one snap when Christian Watson needed a breather. Tight End Josh Whyle: 8 snaps Drake Dabney: 3 snaps While Drake Dabney “started” the game and Josh Whyle didn’t, Whyle out-snapped Dabney with the first-team unit. Generally, Dabney played an in-line position more than Whyle did on Thursday night. Reminder: Tucker Kraft (knee) and Luke Musgrave (neck) were held out of action. Offensive Line Jordan Morgan: 9 snaps (LT) Jager Burton: 9 snaps (LG) Sean Rhyan: 9 snaps (C) Jacob Monk: 9 snaps (RG) Anthony Belton: 9 snaps (RT) Without expected starting right guard Aaron Banks (knee) and starting right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele (knee), Jager Burton and Jacob Monk entered the starting lineup. Monk actually played right guard, pushing expected starting right guard Anthony Belton to right tackle, as the Packers don’t have much tackle depth at the moment. Packers 2nd Team Offense Quarterback Tyrod Taylor: 13 snaps Running Back Pierre Strong Jr.: 7 snaps MarShawn Lloyd: 3 snaps Jaden Nixon: 3 snaps With Lloyd getting all of the work with the first-team unit, Pierre Strong Jr. got the most burn with the second stringers. Notably, undrafted rookie Jaden Nixon got looks ahead of Damien Martinez, a 2025 draft pick who the Packers picked up in December. Receiver Bo Melton: 11 snaps Savion Williams: 11 snaps Skyy Moore: 9 snaps Isaiah Neyor: 4 snaps Bo Melton and Savion Williams were the “starting” outside receivers for the second-team unit, with Skyy Moore playing the role of Jayden Reed — a player who only came onto the field in three-receiver sets, mostly as a slot receiver. Isaiah Neyor got in the mix, but only when Melton and Williams were subbed out for a breather. Tight End Drake Dabney: 11 snaps Messiah Swinson: 5 snaps Dabney got the most looks at tight end with the second-team unit, and apparently Messiah Swinson is the next man up, ahead of McCallan Castles and international exemption Thomas Yassmin, whose first practice with Green Bay was on Family Night. Offensive Line Jordan Morgan: 13 snaps (LT) Jager Burton: 13 snaps (LG) Jacob Monk: 13 snaps (C) Donovan Jennings: 13 snaps (RG) Anthony Belton: 13 snaps (RT) Morgan, Burton, Monk and Belton stayed on the field with the second-team unit, but Monk moved to center as Sean Rhyan was shut down for the day. This opened up a spot at right guard for Donovan Jennings to jump into the lineup. Yes, they all got looks ahead of the likes of Darian Kinnard, John Williams and Travis Glover. Packers 1st Team Defense Defensive Line Karl Brooks: 3 snaps Warren Brinson: 2 snaps Jonathan Ford: 1 snap Both Devonte Wyatt (knee) and Javon Hargrave (knee), the Packers’ most important defensive linemen, weren’t dressed up for the game on Thursday. Jonathan Ford’s snap with the first-team unit came as a 3-4 nose tackle (more on this later), while Karl Brooks and Brinson were the “ends” in that look. Brooks and Brinson also played the nickel snap before the Packers’ first-team defense’s final play: a subpackage where edge rusher Lukas Van Ness kicked into the interior. Brooks was the lone defensive lineman on the field for that rush package. Edge Defender Lukas Van Ness: 3 snaps Barryn Sorrell: 3 snaps Collin Oliver: 1 snap Lukas Van Ness and Barryn Sorrell were the starting edges in this game, and they didn’t get any work after the first-team defense’s three-play drive. Collin Oliver got in the game as a subpackage rusher when Van Ness kicked inside, ahead of Brenton Cox Jr. It’s worth mentioning here that Dani Dennis-Sutton, the Packers’ fourth-round rookie, missed the game with an illness. Off-Ball Linebacker Zaire Franklin: 3 snaps Edgerrin Cooper: 3 snaps Cornerback Keisean Nixon: 3 snaps Brandon Cisse: 3 snaps Safety Xavier McKinney: 3 snaps Evan Williams: 3 snaps Kitan Oladapo: 2 snaps Kitan Oladapo got two snaps with the first-team offense, both in the slot as an injury replacement for Javon Bullard (foot). Packers 2nd Team Defense Defensive Line Warren Brinson: 14 snaps Chris McClellan: 11 snaps Anthony Campbell: 10 snaps Nazir Stackhouse: 10 snaps Jonathan Ford: 7 snaps Jaden Crumedy: 1 snap Again, Ford was used almost exclusively as an odd front nose tackle with the second-team defense, while the rest of the linemen moved around. It seems like the team has a defined role for Ford, unlike the rest of their group — including the big-bodied Nazir Stackhouse. Edge Defender Brenton Cox Jr.: 14 snaps Collin Oliver: 12 snaps Nyjalik Kelly: 10 snaps Arron Mosby: 8 snaps Cox outsnapped Oliver with the second-team unit, even though Oliver got in with the first-team unit in the pressure package. I’m guessing that Nyjalik Kelly and Arron Mosby will get fewer opportunities with the second-team unit when Dennis-Sutton returns to the field. Kelly struggled playing assignment football throughout the night . Off-Ball Linebacker Isaiah McDuffie: 22 snaps Ty’Ron Hopper: 19 snaps The three snaps that Ty’Ron Hopper didn’t play while Isaiah McDuffie was on the field came when Jonathan Gannon called one-linebacker “Penny” packages . Cornerback Keisean Nixon: 17 snaps Brandon Cisse: 17 snaps Benjamin St-Juste: 5 snaps Jaylin Simpson: 5 snaps Keisean Nixon and Brandon Cisse, who played the first-team snaps at outside cornerback, played the first 17 snaps of the second-team defense, too. When they were shut down is when Benjamin St-Juste and Jaylin Simpson got their shot at playing outside cornerback with the second-team unit. All of Simpson’s snaps here came at outside cornerback. He did end up playing some slot reps with the third- and fourth-string defenses later in the game, though. Quick reminder: Carrington Valentine was out with a hamstring and is battling with Cisse and St-Juste for the starting job opposite Nixon. Safety Kitan Oladapo: 22 snaps Mark Perry: 22 snaps Murvin Kenion III: 16 snaps In base 3-4 defense looks, the safeties were Kitan Oladapo and Mary Perry on the second-team defense. When the team played nickel packages, with five defensive backs on the field, Oladapo kicked into the slot, and Murvin Kenion III came off the bench to play safety. Oladapo looked a lot better as a true safety than he did when he was in the slot on Thursday.

full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FL - OCTOBER 27: Head Coach Matt LaFleur of the Green Bay Packers addresses the media during the post game press conference after the game against the Jacksonville Jaguars at EverBank Stadium on October 27, 2024 in Jacksonville, Florida. The Packers defeated the Jaguars 30 to 27. (Photo by Don Juan Moore/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers’ coaching staff, including coordinators and assistants, spoke to the media on Friday following the Packers’ 28-9 preseason loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers. The game was an odd one: Green Bay held the lead with their third-string units (even though it was a bit of a rock match), but when the fourth-string defense entered, they gave up three straight touchdowns to end the game. So what did the Packers’ staff have to say about the performance? Here’s what we got on Friday. First of all, head coach Matt LaFleur said there were no long-term injuries sustained in the game, a great sign. Honestly, that’s probably what fans were hoping the most for going into Thursday’s action. This means that defensive lineman Anthony Campbell and offensive lineman Darian Kinnard, the two players who dropped out of play and did not later return to the field, should be good to go in the near future. That’s big, considering that Kinnard is projected to make the 53-man roster and Campbell is on the roster bubble right now, fighting for the sixth defensive line spot with Jonathan Ford and Nazir Stackhouse. When rookie guard Jager Burton, who started at left guard with Aaron Banks and Zach Bako-Bewele out of the starting lineup yesterday, was brought up, LaFleur mentioned that Burton and Jacob Monk, who started at right guard, are making it “extremely difficult” for the team to simply hand the left guard job back to 2025 starter Aaron Banks once he’s healthy. Before this comment, it was assumed that the Packers’ preferred starting offensive line during the regular season would be Jordan Morgan, Banks, Sean Rhyan, Anthony Belton and Bako-Bewele. Belton has started at right tackle as Bako-Bewele’s injury replacement, but maybe that’s just Green Bay’s attempt at getting their “best five” on the field, rather than where players will be lining up in the regular season. When LaFleur was asked about whether or not Banks had surgery, he simply stated, “I’ll let him answer that,” leading to speculation online that Banks may have had surgery that the Packers did not approve of. Again, that’s just speculation as of now. Banks is dealing with an undisclosed knee injury, for what that’s worth. The offensive line rotation might be even more interesting than we originally thought. On the defensive side of the ball, there was universal praise for rookie cornerback Brandon Cisse and how he carries himself as a 21-year-old professional. New secondary coach/passing game coordinator Bobby Babich, who came to Green Bay after being the Buffalo Bills’ defensive coordinator, stated plainly that there is a cornerback competition, but that returning starter Keisean Nixon has been taking coaching “great.” In all likelihood, Cisse, Carrington Valentine (who missed Week 1 of the preseason with a hamstring injury) and free agent signing Benjamin St-Juste are going to keep battling for the spot opposite Nixon up until (at least) Week 1 of the regular season. DeMarcus Covington, who was previously the Packers’ defensive line coach and run game coordinator under Jeff Hafley’s 4-3 defense, has been promoted to the title of outside linebackers coach/run game coordinator/assistant head coach — defense under Jonathan Gannon’s new 3-4 defense. Covington said that edge defender Lukas Van Ness, who was involved in a sack in one of the three snaps that the defensive starters played on Thursday, is “one of our best players” when he’s healthy. Defensive line coach Vince Oghobaase, who was Covington’s assistant defensive line coach under Hafley, also praised Campbell, who he said has recorded 10 to 12 batdowns at the line of scrimmage throughout camp. Overall, the coaching staff seemed pretty happy with their top two units, while admitting that the team needed to work on tackling. Gannon said that this was just the second live tackling opportunity that the team has had, with the other one being the reserve units’ series on Family Night last week.
author: Justis Mosqueda

title: Kicker Trey Smack already in rare company in recent Packers history
summary: One field goal does not a kicker make. Two feels a lot better, but it’s still not enough for a trend. All that to say, Trey Smack got off to a pretty good start during the Packers’ first preseason game of 2026. Though it didn’t count, Smack opened his Packers career with a 58-yard boot […]
full_text: Aug 13, 2026; Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, USA; Green Bay Packers place kicker Trey Smack (28) kicks a field goal against the Pittsburgh Steelers during the third quarter at Acrisure Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Charles LeClaire-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect One field goal does not a kicker make. Two feels a lot better, but it’s still not enough for a trend. All that to say, Trey Smack got off to a pretty good start during the Packers’ first preseason game of 2026. Though it didn’t count, Smack opened his Packers career with a 58-yard boot to put them up 3-0. A penalty took the points off the board, but we all saw it. It went up and through, easy as you please. Then, after Kyle McCord navigated a tidy two-minute drill at the end of the first half, Smack did it again, putting another 58-yard attempt through the uprights. This one was penalty free, and pulled the Packers to within a point heading into the halftime break. A 38-yard field goal capped Smack’s day, but it’s been enough to get people talking. And they should be. To this point, the story on Smack has been his shaky start to camp, and admittedly, it wasn’t great. The sixth round pick converted just eight of his first 13 attempts in camp, a bad enough start to the season for a kicker of any status to draw heat, much less a rookie who the Packers burned two picks moving up to select. But Smack’s big leg has always been his signature. He set the record at Florida with 10 career field goals of 50 yards or more, and he stood out among kicking prospects for his ability to convert from distance . Even if Brian Gutekunst didn’t go into the draft planning to target a kicker , things fell his way and the Packers put together a package to get him. And now the move is paying early dividends. In a league where attempts from 50+ yards are skyrocketing, having a kicker who can’t put through long kicks is a liability. Though Brandon McManus stabilized the Packers’ kicking game in 2024, it was clear by the end of the 2025 season that he couldn’t get the job done from deep. It’s true that an injury hampered much of his 2025 season, but at age 34, McManus didn’t have the leg he once did, and it cost the Packers. Yes, a 55-yard attempt in Chicago in January is a high-difficulty kick, but a more powerful kicker would have had a better shot at it, and McManus didn’t get the job done when called upon. That’s the brutal evaluation process for kickers: the ball either goes through those tall yellow things or it doesn’t. Put it through, you’re a good kicker. Miss, and you take the blame, regardless of the degree of difficulty. Now, though, it looks like the Packers have a kicker comfortable with distance. Smack’s dual 58-yard boots would have tied for the fourth-longest attempts of the Matt LaFleur era, and his first attempt would have been the longest that didn’t come at the end of a half or game. Brandon McManus attempted a 64-yard field goal to tie the game at the end of the Packers’ 2025 loss to the Eagles, Anders Carlson tried from 63 yards to end the first half during a 2023 game against the Lions, and Lukas Havrisik tried (and made) a 61-yard field goal against the Cardinals in 2025 . Even if it’s just one kick, it seems noteworthy that the Packers even wanted to try. Would they have done the same in a regular season game that counted? Perhaps not, but now they know that Smack can convert from a pretty significant distance when called upon. And for good measure, Smack went ahead and did it twice. That’s a much better place to be than the uncertainty he faced earlier in camp.
author: Jon Meerdink

title: Packers fans still favor Anthony Belton to start at right guard
summary: On Thursday night, the Green Bay Packers played a game for the first time this preseason, giving other teams and their own fans the first look at a potential lineup. Several key players sat out in the team’s exhibition debut against the Pittsburgh Steelers, including starting right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele, but there were several notable […]
full_text: CHICAGO, IL - JANUARY 10: Jacob Monk #62 of the Green Bay Packers runs across the field during an NFC Wild Card Playoff game against the Chicago Bears at Soldier Field on January 10, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Thursday night, the Green Bay Packers played a game for the first time this preseason, giving other teams and their own fans the first look at a potential lineup. Several key players sat out in the team’s exhibition debut against the Pittsburgh Steelers, including starting right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele, but there were several notable developments across the offensive line after the first two weeks of training camp. The right guard position has been one of the most unpredictable spots in the lineup so far, and that continued to be the case through Thursday’s game. Earlier this week, we at Acme Packing Company asked our readers who you expect to start at that position in week one, and there was a clear first and second tier of options in the results: Second-year pro Anthony Belton, who was the team’s starting right guard in the late stages of last season, earns the nod as the overall favorite to start, but he failed to clear 50 percent of the vote at just 46%. Following him are the duo of rookie Jager Burton and third-year pro Jacob Monk at 26 and 21 percent, respectively, while Darian Kinnard landed a distant 3%, behind “other” at six percent. Interestingly, the top three vote-getters in this poll were all members of the starting lineup on Thursday. Belton actually got the nod at right tackle in Bako-Bewele’s place, while Burton played Aaron Banks’ left guard and Monk got the start at the contested right guard spot. Monk then shifted over to center after the first series, when the team gave starter Sean Rhyan a rest, and Donovan Jennings stepped in at right guard instead. Meanwhile, the Packers’ continued cross-training of Belton at both guard and tackle is starting to make it more difficult to pin him down as a potential starter, as it appears he is the top option to back up Bako-Bewele. Would the team rather have him as a swing backup at both spots on the right side with a different player in the starting lineup at guard? It’s tough to say, but after playing all of his snaps at tackle on Thursday night, that seems plausible. In any case, the Packers need a cohesive offensive line if they want to have a chance to win a division title this season. According to FanDuel Sportsbook, the Packers still have the second-best odds to win the NFC North at +260, trailing only the Detroit Lions (+150).
author: Evan "Tex" Western

title: Kyle McCord seems well ahead of Kyron Drones for Packers third QB job
summary: The top end of the Packers’ quarterback depth chart is set. As of last night, we can probably say the same about the bottom end, too. In action against the Pittsburgh Steelers, Kyle McCord looked much more game-ready than fellow low-end quarterback Kyron Drones, whose only real selling point is his athleticism. McCord completed 12 […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - AUGUST 13: Kyle McCord #18 of the Green Bay Packers looks to pass during the third quarter against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Acrisure Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Joe Sargent/Getty Images) | Getty Images The top end of the Packers’ quarterback depth chart is set. As of last night, we can probably say the same about the bottom end, too. In action against the Pittsburgh Steelers, Kyle McCord looked much more game-ready than fellow low-end quarterback Kyron Drones, whose only real selling point is his athleticism. McCord completed 12 of 16 passes for 105 yards on the night. He failed to throw a touchdown and took two sacks, but otherwise avoided any catastrophic errors across his 32 snaps. While he clearly doesn’t have a big arm, McCord showed enough arm strength to get the job done last night, and just as importantly, he maintained a good degree of composure while the Packers’ deep backups on the offensive line surrendered pressure after pressure. The same can’t be said for Drones, who had quite an, um, adventurous six snaps at quarterback. He threw incomplete on his one passing attempt and took three sacks, including one where he ran backwards for 17 yards, bumping the Packers back from their own 22 to their own five-yard line. On another sack, Drones appeared to get spooked when he faced pressure on what looked to be a screen pass . One of them was a screen btw pic.twitter.com/iCAhGDs1oo — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) August 14, 2026 On the one hand, that’s understandable — I can’t say that I’d do anything other than panic if I saw a trio of NFL-sized defensive linemen bearing down on me with ill intent. On the other, that’s part of the gig, man! And you know they’re coming free, because it’s a screen play! Drones was never exactly a polished NFL prospect. Running an option and RPO-heavy scheme at Virginia Tech, Drones only completed a shade over 58% of his career passes, never showing the kind of touch that would indicate he could develop into an NFL-caliber passer. He was certainly a threat with his legs, rushing for more than 1,800 yards as a Hokie, but the days where a quarterback can make it in the NFL as a runner alone are almost a century past. The thinking on a prospect like Drones is that you keep him around on the practice squad to help you prepare for mobile quarterbacks throughout the year. In a division with Caleb Williams and Kyler Murray, that’s certainly something that could interest the Packers. But based on last night (and what we know about the two players in general), this is a situation where the Packers would probably need to justify keeping both McCord and Drones as they fill out their roster. That’s easier than ever on a 16-man practice squad, but is it worth it? I’d argue probably not. Better to keep McCord and keep up the search for a fleet-footed quarterback that can give you anything at all as a passer. If there ever was a race for the third-string quarterback spot, it’s over now.
author: Jon Meerdink

title: Jordan Morgan looks at home back at his natural left tackle spot
summary: Most of what we see in preseason NFL games doesn’t matter at all, as many of the snaps that are taken up by players in those games are from players who won’t play more than special teams snaps during the season. However, with the some members of the Green Bay Packers’ first-team offensive line getting […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - NOVEMBER 10: Jordan Morgan #77 of the Green Bay Packers looks on during the national anthem prior to an NFL football game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Lambeau Field on November 10, 2025 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Most of what we see in preseason NFL games doesn’t matter at all, as many of the snaps that are taken up by players in those games are from players who won’t play more than special teams snaps during the season. However, with the some members of the Green Bay Packers’ first-team offensive line getting extra snaps in week one, there are very important snaps to be watched there. First and foremost, that is the case for new starting left tackle Jordan Morgan. Morgan has struggled somewhat in his career thus far, which has come overwhelmingly playing right guard. That position does not befit his skillset, but due to necessity he ended up playing there for much of his first two seasons. Last season, through both pre-season and the week 18 matchup against Minnesota, Morgan showed much more comfort at his traditional home of left tackle, and that largely continued in the first preseason game of 2026. There isn’t a lot to write home about with Morgan in this game, and I mean that as a compliment. The best thing you can say about an offensive lineman is that you don’t notice him at all, and that’s basically what happened in every snap of this game, bar a few. The best one being Morgan finding the poor soul who found himself in a run fit he didn’t want to be in. This poor DB didn't want to be in the run fit pic.twitter.com/4vuryI3kGg — rcon14 (@rcon14) August 14, 2026 Picking on corners in the box isn’t a traditional part of the job, but it makes for fun clips. On the downside, I think this is the only bad snap from Morgan the entire game, and I’m not even 100% sure it’s on him since for some reason we don’t get an endzone view of this play. This looks like outside zone toss, so Morgan should in theory be working down the line of scrimmage and up to the second level to meet Patrick Queen (#6), the play-side linebacker. Instead, after giving a quick hand to the left guard, Morgan works to seal the back-side linebacker in, but center Sean Rhyan has already beaten him to the spot, which makes sense because in outside zone, this would be Rhyan’s responsibility. Wish they had an endzone view of this play so I could see the leverage of the LB better. Someone blocked the wrong dude. pic.twitter.com/46ohopceJf — rcon14 (@rcon14) August 14, 2026 I could clip the rest of the reps, but it’s mostly just textbook execution. Morgan gets nice push on some combo blocks with the guards, seals his own guy on multiple runs, and allows zero pressures in the pass game. The pressures part is once again notable; across 107 left tackle snaps between last pre-season, the week 18 Vikings game, and last night’s game, Jordan Morgan has allowed one total pressure. Morgan is listed by PFF with two allowed, but one of those is an aborted play by Clayton Tune that they still haven’t updated because they apparently hate me, personally. That gives us a pressure rate allowed of 0.93%. Not 9.3%. 0.93%. Is Morgan going to post a sub-one percent pressure rate in the regular season? Not unless he’s a first ballot Hall of Famer. But the fact his pass protection has been so strong back at his home of left tackle is extremely encouraging for the Packers offensive line this season. The biggest outstanding question for me is his effectiveness in the run game, a place where Rasheed Walker struggled mightily. If Morgan can be closer to average in that department and be a plus-pass blocker, Green Bay will have a real stew going at offensive tackle.
author: rcon14

title: Packers should open up wide receiver competition
summary: There’s a curious phenomenon going on at the moment with the Packers’ wide receiver room: it lacks size.  Anybody who’s watched the Packers throughout the Matt LaFleur era would tell you that’s a bit strange. LaFleur has long preferred big-bodied receivers who can run block, and has been willing to trade speed for size to […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - AUGUST 23: Isaiah Neyor #80 of the Green Bay Packers during the fourth quarter of an NFL preseason football game against the Seattle Seahawks at Lambeau Field on August 23, 2025 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images There’s a curious phenomenon going on at the moment with the Packers’ wide receiver room: it lacks size. Anybody who’s watched the Packers throughout the Matt LaFleur era would tell you that’s a bit strange. LaFleur has long preferred big-bodied receivers who can run block, and has been willing to trade speed for size to enforce his will in the ground game. But right now, Christian Watson is the only noteworthy wide receiver who fits that description, though, to be fair, he might be the best example of a height/weight/speed prospect at the position in recent Packers history. Outside of Watson, though, there’s nothing there. Jayden Reed and Matthew Golden will never be mistaken for hulking specimens, and toward the bottom end of the depth chart, Bo Melton and Skyy Moore make their respective livings either playing bigger than they’re listed or by embodying the traits that make small receivers interesting in their own right. Savion Williams is the one non-Watson exception, except here’s the problem: if we’re talking about wide receivers, I’m not sure Williams really merits a mention, because he really isn’t one. I don’t quite know yet what he is, and I don’t think the Packers do, either, but a receiver he is not. The book on Williams pre-draft in 2025 was that he was a gigantic athlete who was still learning the nuances of the position. A year later (and with essentially half a season of evidence), that seems to still be the case. Williams is, at best, an unrefined wide receiver prospect. If you want to be less generous, you might say he looks more like a super athletic dude that someone put in a uniform and turned loose on a football field. Yes, he technically looks like he belongs, but only because he’s an athlete among athletes. But the Packers do have a couple of big-bodied prospects who look like they can actually play the position. Isaiah Neyor and J. Michael Sturdivant both fit the bill of a height/weight/speed prospect, and both looked much more confident in their abilities on Thursday night. Neyor, who actually appeared in the Packer’s playoff loss to the Bears last season, stands a hair over 6-foot-4 and weighs 218 pounds. You won’t be surprised to learn that he posted terrific numbers in his pre-draft workouts in 2025 before landing with the Packers as an undrafted free agent. Sturdivant, meanwhile, is a slightly lighter, slightly shorter, slightly faster prospect , though still comfortably falling into the “big receiver” category. He also caught our Paul Noonan’s notice for his limited but still impressive productivity in college . Across 37 snaps on Thursday night, Neyor caught four passes for 34 yards, leading the Packers in both categories. Sturdivant played 26 and grabbed two passes for 26 yards. But, more importantly, both looked smooth, calm, and in control when they were on the field. It’s such a squishy, old-school, tobacco-spitting scout way of putting it, but they both looked like football players out there. They knew what to do and when to do it. They have the nuance of the position figured out. Williams doesn’t. Not yet, at least. And although the chances he gets cut are exceptionally slim as a second-year third round pick, if the Packers want actual wide receiver abilities from a big-bodied prospect, looking at other prospects might be wise. Neyor and Sturdivant both look better equipped to contribute than Williams. Maybe they end up starting the year on the practice squad. But if Williams can’t figure out how to play like an actual wide receiver instead of an oversized Tyler Ervin-esque gadget man, it’s likely they won’t stay there for long.
author: Jon Meerdink

title: Green Bay Packers News: Trey Smack stars in preseason debut
summary: For many football players, the cliché goes that everything changes when the pads go on in training camp. For kickers, however, it’s what you do in games, not in practices, that is what matters. If that’s the case, Trey Smack might be just fine. The Green Bay Packers rookie has had an up-and-down spring and […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - AUGUST 13: Head coach Matt LaFleur of the Green Bay Packers (L) talks with head coach Mike McCarthy of the Pittsburgh Steelers after the Steelers' 28-9 win at Acrisure Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Joe Sargent/Getty Images) | Getty Images For many football players, the cliché goes that everything changes when the pads go on in training camp. For kickers, however, it’s what you do in games, not in practices, that is what matters. If that’s the case, Trey Smack might be just fine. The Green Bay Packers rookie has had an up-and-down spring and summer so far, with a few high-profile misses and rough days in practice. However, in the Packers’ preseason debut against the Pittsburgh Steelers on Thursday night, Smack showed why the team traded up to select him in the 6th round of this spring’s NFL Draft. All Smack did was hit every single kick he attempted, as he went 4-for-4 on the night (though one did not end up officially counting due to a penalty on old friend Dean Lowry that gave the Packers a new set of downs). It wasn’t just a perfect night, either — two of those kicks came from 58 yards, they went in opposite directions, and they came at Acrisure Stadium, a notoriously difficult field for kickers. In short, it was everything one could hope for from a rookie kicker’s debut. Sure, the Packers lost the game 28-9. But that’s not important. Smack’s performance absolutely is, as was the job that the starters did in their brief playing time last night and the avoidance of any major injuries. By those metrics, Thursday’s game was a success. Game recap: 5 takeaways from Packers’ preseason loss to Steelers | Packers.com The starters played one series each on offense and defense and they looked solid, with a field goal on the opening drive and a three-and-out defensively. Later, Kyle McCord showed some poise in a few tough situations with the 3rd team offense. Rookie Trey Smack provides ‘highlight of the night’ for Packers in preseason opener | Packers Wire Of course, it was Smack who had the biggest performance of the night, hitting four field goals including two from 58 yards (though only one of those two officially counted due to a penalty on Pittsburgh). Seeing him turn it on and excel under pressure is a great sign amid some mixed results in practice so far. Packers Crushed by Steelers, But Here Are the Three Things That Mattered | SI.com Yes, the reserves on defense looked completely lost as they gave up three touchdowns late, but the performance by the starters in that opening three-and-out was great. It also helped that Lukas Van Ness contributed a big pressure that led to a sack by Zaire Franklin. 2026 NFL Preseason, Week 1: What We Learned from Thursday’s games | NFL.com Even the national narrative coming out of this game was about Smack’s excellent performance. High school football player in Arkansas practices with a venomous snake in his helmet | AP.com Always check your helmet before putting it on — you never know who might have been using it. Packers News in the Feed This is encouraging news. Anthony Campbell and Darian Kinnard were the only two notable injuries in Thursday’s game, but at least Campbell is not expected to miss any significant time. Surely that’s a big relief for him as he tries to earn a spot on the 53. The Feed is the place for you to share whatever it is you want to talk about, big or small. author: Evan "Tex" Western

title: Green Bay Packers Roster: Post-Preseason Week 1 53-man projection
summary: It’s time to update our Green Bay Packers roster prediction, now that we’ve seen the team play some real live-action tackle football in the preseason. The starting offense played only nine snaps against the Pittsburgh Steelers, and the starting defense got just three reps, but we got a good look at the team’s second- through […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OH - AUGUST 11: Green Bay Packers Defensive Lineman Jonathan Ford (99) runs on to the field for the start of the NFL pre-season football game between the Green Bay Packers and the Cincinnati Bengals on August 11, 2023, at Paycor Stadium in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Michael Allio/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images It’s time to update our Green Bay Packers roster prediction, now that we’ve seen the team play some real live-action tackle football in the preseason. The starting offense played only nine snaps against the Pittsburgh Steelers, and the starting defense got just three reps, but we got a good look at the team’s second- through fourth-string units on Thursday. Based on all the information we have right now, here’s our best stab at the Packers’ Week 1 roster. If you want to thumb through our previous predictions, here’s what we had coming out of the draft and Green Bay’s Family Night practice from last week . Quarterback Jordan Love Tyrod Taylor This one seems pretty cut and clear. Ever since Desmond Ridder was cut and veteran quarterback Tyrod Taylor was brought in, it’s been Taylor’s job to lose. While the second-team offense didn’t score against the Steelers, it was Taylor who took the second-team snaps under center, and there’s really been no indication of Kyle McCord, the Packers’ third-stringer, taking away some of those reps during training camp. Running Back Josh Jacobs MarShawn Lloyd Chris Brooks Now that Chris Brooks has returned to practice from his hamstring injury and has officially been taken off the non-football injury list, I’m more confident that this trio is going to be the Packers’ backfield going into Week 1. The X-factor here is whether or not Josh Jacobs will face a suspension from the league or not. If so, Pierre Strong Jr. will likely be the next man up in this unit. Potential discipline looms over a group of NFL players, including Rams WR Puka Nacua and Packers RB Josh Jacobs. Cc: @tyschmit 🎧 https://t.co/mTwS98lcWO pic.twitter.com/e5fW2ZoQwV — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) August 11, 2026 Receiver Christian Watson Matthew Golden Jayden Reed Savion Williams Bo Melton Skyy Moore J. Michael Sturdivant For the first time, mostly because of the lack of depth in the secondary, I think seven receivers are really in play for the Packers. J. Michael Sturdivant can help Green Bay as a non-returner on special teams, a role that few receivers have played in Green Bay under head coach Matt LaFleur (notably, Bo Melton and former Packer Malik Heath have been guys that did so). Strudivant’s combo of size and speed, plus history as a special teams contributor in college (he was the lead blocker for Florida’s kick return unit), could be the difference between him and Isaiah Neyor being WR7. Tight End Tucker Kraft Josh Whyle Drake Dabney I still think that the way the coaching staff and front office have talked about Luke Musgrave’s neck injury means that it’s going to be tough to assume that Musgrave won’t start the year on the physically unable to perform list, which would mean that he’d be out until at least Week 5. If Musgrave is out, Drake Dabney has been the “starting” Y tight end with Tucker Kraft and Musgrave out of practice. I think he’d be the next man up, if the team answers this issue internally. I wouldn’t be surprised if the team looks for a Dabney replacement on the waiver wire, though. Offensive Line Jordan Morgan (LT) Aaron Banks (LG) Sean Rhyan (C) Anthony Belton (RG/RT) Zach Bako-Bewele (RT) Jacob Monk (G/C) Jager Burton (LG) Donovan Jennings (G/C) John Williams (LT/G/C) Darian Kinnard (RT/RG) I don’t think anyone’s stock has sunk quite as badly as Travis Glover’s. Going into last summer, when Glover suffered a season-ending shoulder injury, it seemed like he was going to have a big opportunity to be the team’s true swing tackle in 2025. Now, five backup offensive linemen got in with the second-team unit for the Packers in their preseason opener before him. At one point, I had him projected as the 7th offensive lineman on the team. Now, I think he’s probably sitting in the 11th spot, which might not make the 53-man roster. Darian Kinnard was hurt in Green Bay’s Week 1 preseason game against the Steelers, but we still don’t know what his status is moving forward. If he had a significant injury, I could see Glover taking his spot. Rookie UDFA Dillon Wade is another option. Defensive Line Devonte Wyatt Javon Hargrave Karl Brooks Warren Brinson Chris McClellan Jonathan Ford Here’s a change: I think Jonathan Ford makes the roster if it were decided today. He made some plays on both Family Night and in the preseason opener, which he started at the nose tackle position. Yes, Devonte Wyatt and Javon Hargrave were both held out of action in Week 1 of the preseason, but it was Ford who started between Warren Brinson and Karl Brooks, not other options like Nazir Stackhouse or Anthony Campbell. Campbell left the Steelers game with a lower body injury, but it appears that he will be okay . Campbell lingers in the roster bubble conversation, but it should worry Stackhouse more that Ford, a true nose tackle, is passing him up in that role. Also, I assume that Jordon Riley (coming off an Achilles tear) will start the season on the PUP list. Edge Rusher Lukas Van Ness Barryn Sorrell Brenton Cox Jr. Dani Dennis-Sutton Collin Oliver This is pretty much basically what everyone is going to expect the pass-rusher room to be, barring injuries, now that everyone has accepted that Micah Parsons will start the year on the PUP list. Arron Mosby, a special teams stud, has the chance to get called up from the practice squad at some point during 2026, but I doubt that he’ll make the team in Week 1. As a vested veteran, Mosby would be guaranteed his full salary for the 2026 season if he makes the initial 53-man roster, even if he’s later released by the team. Linebacker Zaire Franklin Edgerrin Cooper Isaiah McDuffie Ty’Ron Hopper Nick Niemann Again, this is another chalk position. Zaire Franklin is the starting Mike, and Isaiah McDuffie is the backup Mike. Edgerrin Cooper is the starting Will, and Ty’Ron Hopper is the backup Will. Nick Niemann is a special teams ace, and both McDuffie and Hopper will contribute on special teams, too. The next man up will be Kristian Welch, another primary special teamer, if there’s an injury at the position. Cornerback Keisean Nixon Carrington Valentine Brandon Cisse Benjamin St-Juste Domani Jackson I’m keeping Kamal Hadden off this list for now, just because of his post-injury performance (he broke two bones and has dealt with two dislocations since December 27th) being a question mark. Domani Jackson and Carrington Valentine are both expected to return to team drills soon, which means that Hadden will likely get buried even further down the depth chart soon. There’s been some buzz on a potential Carrington Valentine trade as of late, but I don’t think the Packers are too interested in moving off of a cheap, young cornerback. Jaylin Simpson, who has been the next cornerback up while Valentine, Jackson and Hadden have been banged up, put up some bad tape at both outside cornerback and in the slot against the Steelers on Thursday. Safety Xavier McKinney Evan Williams Javon Bullard Kitan Oladapo Generally, the Packers like to keep five safeties on the team because they rely on the position heavily on special teams. With Chris Brooks, J. Michael Sturdivant, Benjamin St-Juste and Domani Jackson all being safety-like body types who can contribute on teams, though, I’m not sure Green Bay will be forced to keep five at the position this year. Johnathan Baldwin injuring his knee and being waived with an injury designation was a huge moment for the safety room. Baldwin was set to be the team’s fifth safety, backup slot defender and an occasional special teams contributor. Without Baldwin, I’m not sure that the Packers have another roster-worthy safety. Right now, their…
