title: Raiders’ rookie Treydan Stukes isn’t your run-of-the-mill safety
summary: Announced as a safety when his name was called up at the podium of the 2026 NFL Draft, the Las Vegas Raiders appear set to not pigeon hole second-round pick Treydan Stukes. This particular Arizona Wildcat played a wide array of roles in the secondary and as our Matt Holder explored at the tail end […]
full_text: HENDERSON, NEVADA - MAY 02: Treydan Stukes #31 of the Las Vegas Raiders runs drills during the team's rookie minicamp at the Las Vegas Raiders Headquarters/Intermountain Health Performance Center on May 02, 2026 in Henderson, Nevada. (Photo by David Becker/Getty Images) | Getty Images Announced as a safety when his name was called up at the podium of the 2026 NFL Draft, the Las Vegas Raiders appear set to not pigeon hole second-round pick Treydan Stukes. This particular Arizona Wildcat played a wide array of roles in the secondary and as our Matt Holder explored at the tail end of April, the versatile ballhawk’s penchant to create turnovers is sorely needed in Las Vegas. The lack of takeaways is indeed glaring, as was the Raiders’ need for more talent at safety — particularly the free safety spot. While Stukes has the ability to play the role as a deep safety, his collegiate snaps were very limited in that regard. According to Pro Football Focus (PFF), the 6-foot-2 and 200-pound defensive back truly encompassed that generalization as he notched 1,174 snaps at nickel cornerback, 943 snaps at outside/boundary cornerback, 464 as a box defender (strong safety/linebacker), and lastly 39 as a deep safety in split looks. Thus, a traditional, run-of-the-mill safety Stukes is not. But it’s that versatility the Arizona native possesses that made him the prospect to select with the 38th overall pick in the draft this past April. “Yeah, I’m super grateful for that. I pride myself on trying to be a smart football player, and I’m glad that they see it the same way,” Stukes said after the Raiders’ training camp practice this past Friday, when asked about the confidence coaches have in him to take on different roles. “I want to be able to help the team with things in any way I can, and if that means learning multiple positions, then I’ll keep doing that.” It’s no secret that Stukes had a slow start to camp where he was relegated to second- and even third-team snaps. He’s ramped up first-team looks as of late but that shouldn’t be surprising. His hybrid role of nickel and safety positions is complex but he’s gaining confidence. Also compounding that is having an elite nickel cornerback in Taron Johnson and veteran Isaiah Pola-Mao at the free safety spot. That all noted, the lack of first-team reps for Stukes isn’t overly concerning — yet. Treydan Stukes has worked with the 2s throughout #Raiders camp. Nickel’s will be asked to do so much in Rob Leonard’s defense so they’re likely bringing him along slowly. It feels like he’ll start to make a push next week after they’ve completed their full install on both sides… pic.twitter.com/4kUG1clucj — Jesse Merrick – Silver & Black Sports Network (@JesseSBSN) August 6, 2026 Shining “Star” In defensive coordinator Rob Leonard’s scheme, the nickel cornerback is dubbed as a “star” chess piece that’s able to cover, drop the hammer as a tackler, and bring the pain as an active blitzer. The coverage versatility entails matching up with slot receivers, tight ends, and even running backs and being able to play close to the line of scrimmage and rotating back to the deep safety spot or dropping into zone to disguise the play call. Being a sound physical tackler is vital as the nickel corner in Leonard’s system acts as an extra front-seven defender that can fill gaps and make stops in space. Lastly, by leveraging timing, angles, and protection gaps, the star defender is often asked to blitz to help stymie the run or pressure/drop the quarterback. These are traits that Johnson — acquired via trade from the Buffalo Bills on March 8 — excelled at over the course of his eight seasons in the league (all with Buffalo) since being drafted in the fourth round (121st overall) of the 2018 draft out of Weber State. The role is punishing on the player’s body, however, as the 5-foot-11, 192-pound, 30-year-old veteran has missed games throughout his career with various ailments. Stukes profiles as a bigger and faster (clocked an impressive 4.33-second 40-yard dash time at the NFL Combine) player to man the nickel spot. Thus, athletically, there’s little concern that Stukes can fill the role. It’s the mental part — which is just as taxing as the role is physically — that needs to be equally on par. And it’s something that’s growing with each practice. “I think it’s kind of what you would expect. The game is just a little bit faster, a little more complex. It takes a lot to play this game at a high level. And when you’re trying to learn multiple positions at the same time, it’s a lot of information to take on at once,” Stukes admitted. “I think as you get confident in the scheme and you start to understand the plays as a whole, what we’re trying to accomplish with the calls, that’s when it kind of slows down for you. You can immerse yourself in both positions and be able to help the defense in different ways.” But like Stukes noted above, the confidence the coaching staff has in him is matched by his enthusiasm to be a chess piece in the Raiders’ defense. A scheme that is set to put players in the best possible position succeed. “I think this is a really, really fun scheme to be a part of. I think it gives defensive backs a lot of chances to make plays and a lot of chances to show your talents,” Stukes said. “If you’re good at something, they’re going to make sure that you’re able to do it, and they put you in a spot to do so. So, I think this is a really good scheme and I think it’s going to help our defense.” Treydan Stukes punt defense rep. Klint Kubiak lauded the second-rounder’s effort on special teams so far. pic.twitter.com/gVrTJPVues — Sam Warren (@samwarren83) August 10, 2026 Deciding Depth Having both Johnson and Pola-Mao on the roster gives Las Vegas the opportunity to be straight forward or get creative. But having the two veterans also provides the defensive coaching staff the opportunity to hone and be patient with Stukes’ development. Sure, the 38th overall picking not sprinting forward with pre-dominant first-team snaps can be disconcerting, having an elite nickel corner ahead of him mitigates that. And Pola-Mao, who struggled as a full-time starter at free safety in 2025, is looking to rebound especially on his final year of a two-year contract extension he inked. Ditto for strong safety Jeremy Chinn who is on the final leg of his two-year pact this coming season. At some point, Stukes involvement and snaps will need to exponentially multiply considering Johnson’s age and injury history, alongside both Pola-Mao and Chinn with expiring contracts (sans additional extensions) next offseason. Stukes is certainly taking advantage of having the veterans in front of him. “TJ (Taron Johnson) is a super savvy vet. He’s been playing for a good amount of time and he’s seen a lot. He’s done a lot. He’s played this game at a high level and in that position at high level for a while,” Stukes said. “So, for us to have a guy like that, it’s super helpful. It allows our scheme to do different things. I think he’s a great role model for me in his versatility and how he’s able to help the defense in multiple spots.” Johnson is even shifting to safety in the big nickel sets the Raiders deployed in practices. In those looks, it’s Chinn who moves down into the nickel spot to be a box defender, blitzer, and cover man. Additionally, Stukes isn’t the lone Wildcat on the Raiders roster. Dalton Johnson's versatility is making the late-round rookie a standout with the preseason just a few days away Watch an all-new Upon Further Review with Dalton Johnson 📺 https://t.co/Ead4Yiquch 📰 https://t.co/aLdFlbmRMa pic.twitter.com/crnMRqWK0S — Las Vegas Raiders (@Raiders) August 7, 2026 The team also drafted his collegiate tag team partner, Dalton Johnson, in the fifth round (150th overall). While smaller and slower (4.41 timed speed) than his Arizona teammate, the 5-foot-11 and 198-pound Texas native received first-team looks this offseason so the coaching staff can…

title: Fernando Mendoza passes 1st test in Las Vegas Raiders’ preseason game against Arizona Cardinals
summary: While the Las Vegas Raiders dropped their first preseason game against the Arizona Cardinals 27-14, there’s still a buzz in the Las Vegas air. That’s because quarterback/No. 1 pick of the 2026 NFL draft Fernando Mendoza had a strong Raiders debut, and it’s not like the final score matters in the big picture anyway. As […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - AUGUST 13: Fernando Mendoza #15 of the Las Vegas Raiders looks to pass in the first quarter of a preseason game against the Arizona Cardinals at Allegiant Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Ian Maule/Getty Images) | Getty Images While the Las Vegas Raiders dropped their first preseason game against the Arizona Cardinals 27-14, there’s still a buzz in the Las Vegas air. That’s because quarterback/No. 1 pick of the 2026 NFL draft Fernando Mendoza had a strong Raiders debut , and it’s not like the final score matters in the big picture anyway. As a result, Mendoza leads off the first winners and losers of the 2026 season. WINNER: Fernando Mendoza The Heisman Trophy winner put up a solid stat line, completing 10 of 16 pass attempts (62.5%) for 97 yards and a touchdown with no interceptions . But the numbers don’t even tell the full story. After his first drive, Mendoza settled in and looked comfortable in Klint Kubiak’s offense, consistently working through his reads and finding his checkdowns to take what the defense was giving him and keep the offense on schedule. He also made a handful of smart decisions by throwing the ball away three times, per Pro Football Focus , instead of putting it in harm’s way. Couple that with a few missiles over the middle to fit passes into tight windows, one for a first down and another for a touchdown, and there was plenty to be encouraged about from the No. 1 overall pick in his first NFL game. Fernando Mendoza threading the needle! Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/PC9UPZvRxA — NFL (@NFL) August 14, 2026 LOSER: Jermod McCoy Thursday night was McCoy’s first football game in about two years, so it’s understandable that he looked a little rusty. However, getting beaten on the goal line for two touchdowns can’t be ignored. Also, the Cardinals were three-for-three when targeting him, per PFF , giving up an 11-yard catch in addition to the two scores. The Tennessee product had trouble holding up against physicality at the top of the route versus Arizona’s pass-catchers, as former player and preseason color analyst Kirk Morrison pointed out on the Raiders’ broadcast. So, the good news is McCoy wasn’t getting beaten too badly where he was leaving receivers wide open, but finishing reps stronger should be a point of emphasis moving forward. WINNER: Jack Bech There was a lot of chatter about Bech this offseason, and he silenced some doubters in the first preseason game. The 2025 second-round pick caught all three targets that came his way, and the trio of grabs was impactful, with two going for first downs and one for a touchdown. He also did a good job of bailing out his quarterbacks. Bech’s first catch came on a third down where Kirk Cousins was a little late and didn’t have much heat on the throw, allowing the cornerback to contest the catch with a big hit as the ball arrived. Then, on another third down, Mendoza was slightly off target with a high throw, but the wideout reached up and secured the grab to move the chains. On top of that, Bech had a great crack block on a safety to help spring Mike Washington Jr. on Washington’s 53-yard run. Overall, this was a much-needed performance from the TCU product, who seems to be settling into the WR3 role. Jack Bech 👀👀 https://t.co/VcFix3UAR2 — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) August 14, 2026 LOSER: Hezekiah Masses Along the same lines as McCoy, Masses also had issues in coverage and gave up completions all three times he was targeted against the Cardinals. One was a short curl that resulted in a first down, the second came on third down when he was in off coverage against a slant, and he got boxed out by a bigger receiver for another chain-moving catch. So, it’s not as if the fifth-rounder was giving up big plays, but he also didn’t make any plays to suggest that the training camp hype will translate to the regular season. WINNER: Cian Slone Overall, the Raiders’ pass-rush had a tough night with only seven total pressures, per PFF , on Arizona’s 32 dropbacks. But Slone had a couple of good wins around the edge, one where it looked like there was an uncalled hold and then a nice speed and cross-chop combo to get a sack. He also made a couple of tackles against the run to turn in a solid, well-rounded performance and take a step toward making the team. Cian Slone sack + run stops One UDFA I expect to make a 53 this season pic.twitter.com/kDeWYGV0d1 — NFL Draft Files (@NFL_DF) August 14, 2026 LOSER: Kansei Matsuzawa There’s still a lot of training camp left, but Matt Gay might have won the kicker competition on Thursday night. Matsuzawa had a rough showing, missing a chip-shot field goal from 38 yards and having a kickoff fall short of the landing zone and go out of bounds. Those are the types of mistakes you can’t have as a kicker, especially when accuracy is your calling card. WINNER: Patrick Johnson To be honest, I had never heard Patrick Johnson’s name before the matchup against the Cardinals. But he did a great job of making a name for himself, finishing second on the team in tackles with six and recording one of Las Vegas’ two sacks. According to PFF , Johnson also had two of the Raiders’ seven pressures and was the highest-graded defender with an impressive 89.4 mark. That should put the six-year veteran on the coaching staff’s radar. LOSER: Jackson Powers-Johnson To be fair, Powers-Johnson did have a nice pancake on one of Ashton Jeanty’s runs. However, he had some issues in pass protection by giving up a couple of pressures, including a sack, per PFF . It’s a small sample size with just 21 total snaps and 14 in pass protection. But it doesn’t help that Caleb Rogers was clean in his pass pro opportunities, not surrendering a single pressure on 12 pass blocking snaps. That’s something to keep tabs on as the right guard battle continues. WINNER: Trey Zuhn III Zuhn is firmly in the mix to compete for a starting spot at right tackle, taking 31 snaps at the position on Thursday. He played well too, yielding just one pressure on 20 snaps in pass protection and earning a solid 69.5 run-blocking grade from PFF . The latter is even more significant, seeing as that was one of his question marks coming out of college. DJ Glaze did do his part to keep the job, though, winning every rep in the passing game and posting an 86.3 grade in the running game. Granted, that was on just 10 snaps, so it isn’t an apples-to-apples comparison with Zuhn. But the fact he only participated in the offense’s first drive is a good sign that the coaching staff is liking what they’re seeing from the third-year pro.

summary: There has been an onslaught of players around the NFL getting contracts in recent weeks. It’s been nearly a daily occurrence. Does that mean the Las Vegas Raiders will soon join the extension signing party? Sure, it’s possible, but the Raiders really don’t have a lot of players who are entering the final year of […]
full_text: There has been an onslaught of players around the NFL getting contracts in recent weeks. It’s been nearly a daily occurrence. Does that mean the Las Vegas Raiders will soon join the extension signing party? Sure, it’s possible, but the Raiders really don’t have a lot of players who are entering the final year of their contract to make a priority. Here are the Raiders’ current 2027 unrestricted free agents (UFA): DT Thomas Booker OL Spencer Burford S Jeremy Chinn WR Phillip Dorsett K Matt Gay Edge Malcom Koonce TE Michael Mayer OL Jordan Meredith QB Aidan O’Connell TE Albert Okwuegnunam LB Segun Olubi SAF Isaiah Pola-Mao TE Ian Thomas WR Tre Tucker WR Dareke Young Note: Quarterback Kirk Cousins isn’t a pending free agent, but he is fully expected to be relelsed next year. As it stands today, let’s break down Las Vegas’ current 15 pending unrestricted free agents (Cousins not included). So, there aren’t a lot of obvious extension candidates. I’d say Chinn could be a possiblity. He is a solid play and a he is still in his prime. I know the Raiders drafted two safeties, so they may not feel an urge to secure Chinn beyond this year, though. Players such as Booker, Burford, Gay, Koonce, Mayer and Tucker could get consideration for extensions now, but the team may want to see them all perform some during the season to make those decisions. Of course, the big extension looming for the team is for superstar tight end Brock Bowers. However, he won’t be eligible to re-sign until after his this season.

(Photo by Doug Murray/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Miami Dolphins visit the Washington Commanders on Friday night to kick off the preseason for both teams. The three-game preseason always sparks debates about how much playing time starters should get, especially in the first game. Some teams sit the entire top of their depth chart. Some teams play select starters. And some teams put everyone out there for a short period before moving on to the developmental players. For the Dolphins, a team in a rebuild full of younger players who need to prove themselves and veterans hoping to spark a career rebound, the debate is lively, but we do have some indication of their plan for the starters. Quarterback Malik Willis, signed as a free agent in the offseason, is expected to start. The Palm Beach Post’s Joe Schad seems to think that is a good plan, because Willis, a 2022 third-round pick of the Tennessee Titans who spent the last two seasons with the Green Bay Packers, is essentially one of those younger players who needs to prove himself. This is the fifth NFL season for Miami Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis, but as coach Jeff Hafley correctly notes, “It’s like his rookie year …” That’s because Willis has made only six career starts. title: SB Nation Reacts Results: Short Time for the Vikings’ Starters on Saturday
summary: We have the results of this week’s SB Nation Reacts survey for our Minnesota Vikings for this week, and we have it well ahead of the weekend because it pertains to this weekend’s preseason opener against the New York Football Giants at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. We asked you exactly how long the Vikings’ […]
full_text: EAGAN, MINNESOTA - MAY 27: Dallas Turner #15 of the Minnesota Vikings participates in a drill during an OTA workout at Twin Cities Orthopedics Performance Center on May 27, 2026 in Eagan, Minnesota. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) | Getty Images We have the results of this week’s SB Nation Reacts survey for our Minnesota Vikings for this week, and we have it well ahead of the weekend because it pertains to this weekend’s preseason opener against the New York Football Giants at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. We asked you exactly how long the Vikings’ starters should see the field for against the Giants tomorrow afternoon, and folks seem to think they should see a fairly extensive amount of playing time, at least compared to what we’ve seen in the recent past. Of those who responded to our poll, 48% believe that the starters for the purple should hit the field for at least two series, while another 30% believe that should extend to at least three series (and possibly more). Only 13% believe they should only go out there for one series, while the remaining 9% believe they shouldn’t get on the field at all. Over the past couple of seasons, the Vikings’ starters have seen just about no time during the preseason. Obviously, with the quarterback issue that the team has had in camp, that can’t be the case this preseason. Kevin O’Connell has already said that both Kyler Murray and J.J. McCarthy will play on Saturday, so we’ll have to keep an eye on the extent to which both of them see action. As far as some of the other starters, I’m sure there will be a case-by-case basis for some of them playing or not playing. I would be absolutely stunned if we saw Justin Jefferson in the offensive huddle on Saturday, for example, but a lot of the other starters will probably see at least a little bit of action. Whatever the case may be, we will be here for all of Saturday’s game against the Giants, and we hope that you’ll be here to join us and talk about everything that’s happening. As always, we want to thank everyone that took the time to participate in our poll for this week, and be sure to keep your eyes open for the next one! summary: Ahead of his first training camp as New England Patriots head coach in 2025, Mike Vrabel explained that he was judging his team’s performances by three distinct categories. full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - AUGUST 13: Eli Raridon #82 of the New England Patriots tries to escape from A.J. (Photo by Fred Kfoury III/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Ahead of his first training camp as New England Patriots head coach in 2025, Mike Vrabel explained that he was judging his team’s performances by three distinct categories. There is the good, there is the bad, and there is, as he called it, the s—t that gets you beat. The Patriots’ 13-13 preseason opener against the Indianapolis Colts featured a little bit of all three. And if the coach wants to look at his team through his categorizations, who are we to disagree? So, let’s break down Thursday’s game accordingly. The good: Big plays After struggling during Tuesday’s joint practice, the Patriots’ defensive machinery shifted into a higher gear on Thursday night. Besides giving up only 13 points and allowing the Colts to go just 1-for-8 on third down and 0-for-1 on fourth down, the group also registered four takeaways on the day — all without playing its regular starters. Cornerback Kindle Vildor was first to step up, intercepting a bobbled pass to end Indianapolis’ first possession. In the early second quarter, John Saunders Jr. and Dell Pettus teamed up for a fumble recovery to keep the Colts off the board despite being in a 1st-and-goal situation from the 1-yard line. On the very next drive, K.J. Britt showed some good range to knock the ball out of quarterback Anthony Richardson’s hands with teammate Isaiah Iton falling on it for the recovery. In the third quarter, Saunders Jr. was at it again by picking off a Riley Leonard throw and returning it 26 yards to set up a field goal. At that point in the game, four of the Colts’ seven possessions had ended in turnovers. “The turnovers are great, and I love us attacking the football and taking advantage of that,” said Mike Vrabel after the game. While the defensive big plays were one of the biggest takeaways from the contest, the Patriots also managed to make some big plays on offense. Whether it was Tommy DeVito and Kyle Williams connecting on a 25-yard deep ball or 12-yard touchdown, the unit going 2-for-2 on fourth down, or the disallowed chunk plays we will mention shortly, New England did manage to also have a few big as well as some medium-sized plays on offense. The bad: Untimely penalties The Patriots were flagged five times on the day, resulting in a loss of 35 total yards. Those numbers are not bad, but the timing of the infractions were. Caleb Lomu being flagged for an admittedly harsh ineligible man downfield penalty negated a 25-yard pass to Eli Raridon; Efton Chism illegally blocking above the waist took a 16-yard screen pass to Lan Larison off the board; James Hudson also being too far up the field wiped out a 48-yard Cameron Dorner reception; Lorenz Metz holding on a block turned a 13-yard Hassan Haskins run into a 10-yard penalty. “Unfortunately penalties got a lot of our big plays called back,” said Raridon afterwards. Four of the five penalties came on offense, but the lone defensive infraction also negated a big play. On what would have been a third-down stop on the eventual game-tying field goal drive, Isaiah Iton was flagged for illegal use of hands. The s—t that gets you beat: Insufficient finishing Obviously, Andy Borregales missing three of five field goal attempts including the potential game-winner from 49 yards out is not ideal. In fact, Mike Vrabel stating during his postgame presser that “[w]e expect him to make them” pretty much sums the whole situation up. However, Borregales’ 40% success rate on Thursday is just the tip of the proverbial iceberg. The Patriots in general had trouble with their finishing when in possession of the football. Of their 12 total possessions, six ended in punts — a direct result of them going just 5-of-18 of third downs for a 28% conversion rate. Some of that was due to quarterback Tommy DeVito not being fully on target, including on what could have been a 43-yard touchdown to Kyle Williams in the late second quarter. Hitting plays like these, as well as getting the field goal rate back up, would go a long way toward a game like Thursday’s not remaining close despite a plus-four turnover margin.
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: Patriots Fan Notes from preseason game vs. Colts
summary: Like Odysseus after 10 years at war and 10 more at sea, we’re back. Patriots football is semi-officially underway, and I couldn’t be happier. Even though the Red Sox are suddenly good, ever since the World Cup ended I have been jonesing for some sports that get me riled up in the way that the […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - AUGUST 13: Spencer Shrader #3 of the Indianapolis Colts kicks a field goal to tie the game 13-13 in the second half against the New England Patriots at Gillette Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Jaiden Tripi/Getty Images) | Getty Images Like Odysseus after 10 years at war and 10 more at sea, we’re back. Patriots football is semi-officially underway, and I couldn’t be happier. Even though the Red Sox are suddenly good, ever since the World Cup ended I have been jonesing for some sports that get me riled up in the way that the other football can. We now have a Patriots game every single week until late November, which is just fine with me. Before I get into this year’s Fan Notes in earnest, I need to reverse a potential jinx I may have just put on this team by opening up the season with an Odyssey reference. Because one thing I don’t want to do is associate the New England Patriots with Odysseus in any way. And why is that, you may ask? Well the harsh reality is this: if there’s a more overrated hero in the entire history of literature than Odysseus, I have no idea who that person is. It pains me to say it, because Odysseus is an absolute badass in The Iliad. An excellent speaker and diplomat. A fierce warrior. Courage under pressure. Incredibly intelligent. But The Iliad isn’t really Odysseus’s story; center stage for that one belongs to Achilles. What The Odysse y gives us is the story of a man who, through a combination of poor decision-making, hubris, negligence, recklessness, and sheer arrogance, manages to turn what should have been a relatively pain-free trip home after a brutal war into a decade-long ordeal in which every single one of his men ends up killed, all while he’s getting balied out left and right by a goddess with a deck so stacked in his favor he might as well have been playing Madden on rookie mode against a toddler. And all of this is happening while his poor wife is at home getting bombarded from all angles by a bunch of douchebag suitors. Yet somehow, perhaps through effective marketing and an aggressive advertising campaign (for example, absolutely nowhere in any of the ancient texts is Odysseus explicitly credited with coming up with the idea for the Trojan Horse), everyone puts Odysseus into the GOAT debate of all-time great literary heroes. Well I call shenanigans. OK, I’m done. Sorry about that. Nobody came here for my opinion of a three-thousand-year-old poem or the various literary hills on which I’m willing to die. And Odysseus being the Joe Namath of heroic canon won’t stop me from enjoying the movie when it eventually hits the streaming services (I’m just not a movie theater guy. I think the last flick I saw in theaters was Inception). You’re all here for my hard-hitting analysis of a completely meaningless game in which the starters barely saw the field and a fair number of the players out there last night will be selling insurance by this time next month. So let’s get into that. I just wanted to make sure the 2026 season doesn’t become the story of Mike Vrabel making a bunch of horrible coaching decisions that lands the whole team on the IR. As always, what follows are more random, meandering, completely meaningless observations than they are anything substantive. I didn’t go back and rewatch any game tape, and I’m not going to bother taking the time to learn everyone’s name. We’re all so starved for football by August that it’s easy for these games to feel way more fun than they actually are, but what these games are really about are the back end of the roster, those few surprise players who weasel their way into our hearts, and which guys aren’t out there as opposed to which ones are. That said, early August is the absolute best time to play everyone’s favorite game, “Who the Hell is That Guy?” The 2026 version of this game brings us two Kobe(e)s who both play receiver and both wear No. 19, which makes things extra fun. Some of my favorite “Who the Hell is That Guy?” frontrunners: Mitch Van Vooren. Nick DeGennaro. Peter Manuma. Quintavyvious Hutchins. And perhaps the winner of the preseason thus far, who needs to make the team desperately so he isn’t forced to make a living going out on quests to slay the ancient evils lurking beneath the Forgotten Caves of Eluria: Kindle Vildor. It’s hard not to enjoy Tommy DeVito, who at this point seems to have firmly ensconced himself into that coveted position of Patriots backup quarterback. I couldn’t care less about the stat line—though 13 of 22 for 138 yards and a TD is solid. What I do care about is having fun watching him play two more times and then never seeing him under center again for the rest of the year unless the Patriots are up by four scores with less than five minutes to play. If there are two things that remain consistent in these preseason games, or at least things that you can put some weight in, they are tackling and special teams. Special teams will be a lot of guys’ tickets onto a roster this year, so you’re going to see a lot of effort on those plays. But that will all matter a lot more over the next two games than this one, as that’s when we’ll start seeing the actual units come into shape. I’m not going to panic about the poor tackling and relative lack of run defense yet either. But something to watch going forward. At least that’s what I’m telling myself this morning to justify Andy Borregales’s day. That and the fact that his long snapper was hurt. Yeah, that must have been it. As of right now, I couldn’t for the life of me tell you what the New England WR room is going to look like. There are currently 12 on the roster for what I imagine will be six, maybe seven, spots. And outside of A.J. Brown, would you consider any other player to be a mortal lock? You figure Doubs, Douglas, Hollins, and Williams are locks too… but maybe not? Boutte has been a big trade rumor, but he looks great. Chism stands out at every practice. I’ll say this, though: it’s nice to be writing with a focus on backup quarterbacks and an abundance of offensive weapons in August as opposed to some version of “I wonder if the Patriots are going to have enough players that are actually capable of playing football at a high level.” I’m pulling very hard for Lan Larrison. He has a great football name and an even better mustache. And he was the team’s second-leading receiver last night. I just can’t help but wonder if, as a running back, his seven rushes for one yard are going to end up hurting his chances, particularly in a deep RB room. Did Jam Miller do enough to secure the RB3 spot last night? Of course not. Does he look like the RB right now? For sure. Am I going to be insufferable with my Spaceballs references all season if he does make the team and has an impact? If you even have to ask that question, you haven’t been following my writing for the last decade and a half. Man, I missed Scott Zolak. He seemed more reigned in than usual last night, maybe because it was a very mellow game or maybe because Gillette upped the price of booze again in the offseason. But Zolak is a great example of someone who knows exactly what his place is in the world and is living his best life there. Ben Brown was able to walk to the locker room, for what it’s worth. Hopefully he’ll be OK. No injuries to anyone is all you really want in one of these games. This game has whetted my appetite, and I’m way more excited than I should be for next week, when the starters will likely see some time and we’ll get a better sense of what actual football is. I still don’t know if Week 2 is the new Week 3 of the preseason or not, but I guess it doesn’t really matter. Just everyone stay healthy, and let’s speed on towards September. It’s good to be back writing these. But man am I out of shape. I didn’t think a person could get winded typing on a laptop, but here I find myself. Time to go lie down.
author: Alec Shane

title: Patriots defense shines with 4 takeaways in preseason opener
summary: Four defensive turnovers highlighted a standout performance by the New England Patriots defense during Thursday night’s preseason opener tie against the Indianapolis Colts. The unit notched two interceptions and two forced fumbles in the 13-13 finish. Two of the Patriots’ takeaways came in crucial moments during drives the Colts offense was threatening to score. “I […]
full_text: Aug 13, 2026; Foxborough, Massachusetts, USA; New England Patriots cornerback Kindle Vildor (28) intercepts a pass to Indianapolis Colts wide receiver Coleman Owen (9) during the first half at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Four defensive turnovers highlighted a standout performance by the New England Patriots defense during Thursday night’s preseason opener tie against the Indianapolis Colts. The unit notched two interceptions and two forced fumbles in the 13-13 finish. Two of the Patriots’ takeaways came in crucial moments during drives the Colts offense was threatening to score. “I think they better have, or there would have been a lot more points that [Indianapolis] scored,” head coach Mike Vrabel said after Thursday’s game. “The turnovers are great, and I love us attacking the football and taking advantage of that.” After progressing 52 yards in five plays to open the second quarter, the Colts ran a quarterback sneak with 6-foot-4, 244-pound Anthony Richardson at the one-yard line. Stepping up to the challenge, defensive tackle Jeremiah Pharms Jr. punched the ball loose, ultimately ending up in the hands of safety Dell Pettus. Both players were captains in a matchup where a majority of the starters rested. While Vrabel still sees room for improvement, he acknowledged how drastically turnovers like Pharms’ can alter a contest’s outcome. “Just a lot of things to clean up, but when you talk about the ability to create turnovers, it can change the game,” Vrabel added. “Just try to defend every blade of grass down there on the goal line, and come up with a big turnover there.” On Indianapolis’ following drive, free-agency signing K.J. Britt — with Isaiah Iton recovering — forced another fumble on Richardson as the opposing signal-caller was scrambling into the red zone. A 27-yard punt return by Coleman Owen prior gave the Colts strong field positioning in their attempt to tie at seven apiece. And in its efforts to prevent plays through the air, New England’s two interceptions both came during Indianapolis’ opening drives in each half. Kindle Vildor, who was also a March signing, came away with a mishandled Richardson pass to the quarterback’s receiver in the flat early during the first frame. Furthermore, at the start of the second half, safety John Saunders Jr. jumped a deep ball from Riley Leonard intended for Eli Pancol on a skinny post. Creating more takeaways has been a goal of the Patriots’ secondary throughout training camp. Earlier this offseason, Pettus detailed a challenge that veteran safety Kevin Byard requested from the room after the defense had secured only one takeaway through the first six summer practices. “After those first few practices, [Byard] brought us up, and he was like, ‘We need takeaways today,’” Pettus shared. “Before we went to any competitive team activity, he said, ‘We need more takeaways; we’re going to go out here and go get the football. Forget what everybody else is talking about; forget what the coaches talk about. This is our team. This is our defensive backfield.’ And like, it’s up to us to go get it, because the coaches can’t play for us. And I told him I thought that was great to hear just because he set the tone for us that day.” Later that day, Pettus recorded the defense’s second interception of training camp. That same emphasis on producing turnovers has now carried over from practice and into a game environment on Thursday.

title: Patriots rookie motivated by Mike Vrabel’s in-game challenge
summary: Gabe Jacas had an eventful preseason debut. Not only did the New England Patriots rookie play a combined 37 snaps between defense and special teams, he also registered five total tackles. Three of those takedowns came in the kicking game, which was good enough for the team lead on Thursday night. The output did not […]
full_text: Foxborough, MA - August 4: New England Patriots linebacker Gabe Jacas at training camp on August 4, 2026. (Photo by David L. Ryan/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images Gabe Jacas had an eventful preseason debut. Not only did the New England Patriots rookie play a combined 37 snaps between defense and special teams, he also registered five total tackles. Three of those takedowns came in the kicking game, which was good enough for the team lead on Thursday night. The output did not happen by accident, though. Instead, it was preceded by Mike Vrabel personally challenging Jacas early on. “He was just like, ‘I’m tired of seeing you get blocked,’” the young outside linebacker explained after the Patriots’ 13-13 tie against the Indianapolis Colts . “I was like, ‘S—t, I’m not getting blocked.’ So, that’s what I did. Vrabel demands the best out of his players, so that’s what he did.” According to New England’s head coach, the challenge stemmed from Jacas’ effort on a kickoff coverage play. “I challenged him on a kickoff, and he made a tackle,” Vrabel said. “I didn’t think that his efforts were maybe good enough on the kickoff. I didn’t expect that the guy that was blocking him to be able to block him, and then I challenged him, and he came up with a tackle on the kickoff. So that was a positive, and then we’ll just keep coaching him just like the rest of the guys.” Jacas, the Patriots’ second-round draft selection back in April, was one of several rookies seeing prominent snaps versus the Colts. Seven first-year players started the contest: four on offense and three, including the Illinois product, on the defensive side of the ball. While Jacas’ performance overall had its ups and downs, which is not uncommon for a rookie playing in his first ever game against professionals, he felt good about it. “Just having the opportunity to go out there and play the game of football, I love it,” he said. “Every snap I had, just going out there, running around. Very valuable.”
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: Jam Miller makes case for Patriots’ RB3 role in preseason opener
summary: The New England Patriots continue to search for a third running back behind Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson. In Thursday’s preseason opener against the Indianapolis Colts, seventh-round pick Jam Miller made his case for the role. The rookie totaled 55 yards on 14 carries while breaking a long of 15, with his physicality along the […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - AUGUST 13: Jam Miller #30 of the New England Patriots dives for a first down against Daniel Scott #32 of the Indianapolis Colts in the second quarter at Gillette Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Jaiden Tripi/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New England Patriots continue to search for a third running back behind Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson. In Thursday’s preseason opener against the Indianapolis Colts , seventh-round pick Jam Miller made his case for the role. The rookie totaled 55 yards on 14 carries while breaking a long of 15, with his physicality along the way catching the eye of his head coach. “It was good to see Jam come out and have some nice runs,” Mike Vrabel said post game. “I felt like he ran with his pads down and had a couple physical runs, and was happy for him. This is a great evaluation. We can start to figure out guys that can and start to figure out guys that can’t too.” For the 5-foot-10, 209 pound Miller, physicality is a key part of his game. “I would say aggressive,” Miller said about his play style. “Aggressive with a little bit of speed in it, but I’m just going to do whatever I can do to help this team win.” The Patriots running back room has seen turnover the last two days. Following injuries to Myles Montgomery and Terrell Jennings, the Patriots signed Hassan Haskins and JaMycal Hasty to the roster. With those two joining Miller and Lan Larison, the Patriots will hope to find one capable of spelling their top duo in the regular season. “I think you try to see what you have in the young guys, and then those guys are veterans. They’ve played,” Vrabel said. “They’re probably two different style of backs, but I like both of them personally. We’ve had some experience with JaMycal, and then going back to Tennessee with Hassan. I think it’s probably too early to tell for both of them. I know that they’re going to compete, but we just got them yesterday to be able to get them ready for the game.” The Patriots will return to the practice fields Saturday as they turn the page to a new week. That will bring the Philadelphia Eagles to town for a pair of joint practices and their second preseason game, where Miller will have even more opportunities to separate himself from the pack. “Jam was great,” quarterback Tommy DeVito said. “His confidence, that helps myself and everybody in the huddle believe in him and feel confident — so when we hand him the ball, he lowers his pads. He will lay the boom on somebody. He also has a little shiftiness that I am ready to see some more and more. The more tackling that I get to see him partake in, it will be fun.”
author: Brian Hines

title: 10 things we learned from Patriots vs. Colts NFL preseason game
summary: The New England Patriots played the opening game of their 2026 preseason against the visiting Indianapolis Colts on Thursday night. It might have been a relatively uneventful game ending in a 13-13 tie, but there was still a lot to see and take away from. Some guys seemingly helped themselves, while others had a tough time. […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - AUGUST 13: John Saunders Jr. #23 of the New England Patriots celebrates his interception with his teammates during a game between the New England Patriots and the Indianapolis Colts on August 13, 2026, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Fred Kfoury III/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New England Patriots played the opening game of their 2026 preseason against the visiting Indianapolis Colts on Thursday night. It might have been a relatively uneventful game ending in a 13-13 tie , but there was still a lot to see and take away from. Some guys seemingly helped themselves, while others had a tough time. Let’s sort through all of it and get into our takeaways from the first game of the season. Andy Borregales struggles Andy Borregales has looked great in training camp, but his practice performance did not translate to the field on Thursday. He hit two field goals from 40 and 52 yards, but also missed from quite badly from 55 as well as from 56 and then from 49 at the end of the game to win. He was solid, and clutch, last year, but his first game as a sophomore was rough. The hope is that he gets the misses out of his system, but it was a really bad night for the second-year kicker. Maybe Julian Ashby being hurt and having to work with a backup long snapper hurt the operation, but, they’re professionals, so those misses still shouldn’t happen. I’m not panicking just yet, and neither seems to be head coach Mike Vrabel , but he missed a few field goals during this week’s joint practice, and then missed three on Thursday. That’s not good, and honestly surprising based on what we have seen out of him for most of the summer so far. Injury concerns arise In preseason, you want to see what guys have, get everyone ready to play regular season football, and hopefully come out unscathed on the injury front. The Patriots didn’t manage to accomplish the latter on Thursday. In the first quarter, Ben Brown, who is their top interior backup offensive lineman, went down with an injury . He went from the blue tent to the locker room, which isn’t a good sign. Then, later in the game, Andrew Rupcich got banged up as well even though he remained on the sideline and later gave the all-clear in the locker room. Still, losing two guys at a position where there was already minimal depth is a tough break for the Patriots. The hope is that neither injury is overly serious. Depth O-linemen look good Even though the depth along the offensive line took a hit on Thursday night when Ben Brown and Andrew Rupcich got hurt, I liked what I saw from two depth tackles. Both Marcus Bryant, who played early in the game, and Dametrious Crownover, who played late in the game, had pretty solid games. There’s probably only one spot after Will Campbell, Morgan Moses and Caleb Lomu at tackle, and right now Bryant should have the clear edge, but Crownover looked competent out there too (albeit against worse competition). I wonder if this performance gets him some run with the second unit to see if he can handle himself with them. Either way, for a position group that just got hit by injury, and already had a ton of questions on the interior, it was nice to at least see a few of the depth tackles register solid performances. Tommy DeVito has his ups and downs Second-string quarterback Tommy DeVito got the start for the Patriots, and had flashes where he looked very good, like his long pass to Cam Dorner that was wiped off because of a penalty, and the touchdown and curl route passes to Kyle Williams. He also missed a bunch of throws as well, including what should have been a deep TD to Williams, which he left short. Ultimately, his inconsistency is why he is a backup in the first place, and shouldn’t surprise anyone. That said, he has looked good in camp, so I was thinking that he might have a more consistent night. He’s still a fine backup, but I would be worried if… you know what, never mind, I’m not even going to write those words down. Penalties are a concern On multiple occasions, big plays were wiped off the board because of ineligible man downfield penalties. One, came against rookie OT Caleb Romu and was a little suspect because he was engaged in a block, while the other was called against guard James Hudson. There were a bunch of other penalties on the offense as well, including a holding call on Lorenz Metz in the fourth quarter. Overall, the Patriots finished the day with five accepted penalties for a loss of 35 yards. It is something that they are going to have to fix moving forward. Obviously, they played mostly backups, but you still expect better. Two depth edges flash It is no secret that the Patriots need more help rushing the passer from the edge, and the play of Jesse Luketa and Bradyn Swinson should be a bright spot for the Patriots. Both looked explosive and pressured the Colts’ quarterbacks multiple times; one of Swinson’s disruptions led to a John Saunders Jr. interception, and one of Luketa’s led to a sack by Joshua Farmer. The edge room has a few spots up for grabs, and those two looking good could help at least one of them grab a roster spot. John Saunders Jr. has a really solid performance Safety is another of the spots where the Patriots don’t seem to have a ton of quality depth, but John Saunders Jr. had a nice night. He had multiple run stops, an interception with a good return, and also was credited with a forced fumble when he knocked the ball out at the goal line. It might not have been an actual fumble, but the refs missed it, and the Patriots benefitted from a heads-up play. While Saunders Jr. still appears to be on the outside looking in as far as the 53-man team is concerned. More performances like Thursday’s might help him with his case to get one of the depth spots, though. Cameron Dorner keeps showing up The Patriots have a treasure trove of wide receivers including undrafted rookie Cameron Dorner, who has made plays every day of camp. Thursday night was no different. Dorner didn’t get a ton of opportunities, seeing just three total passes thrown his way. He had a really nice catch on one of those targets that was called back because of a penalty. On the very next play, he caught a screen for a first down. Dorner only had one other target, where the defender made a good play on a back-shoulder throw that came in a little high, but what we saw from him was solid. I thought it was also notable that he barely played in the second half, meaning that it looks like he might be a tier ahead of the receivers that were playing with third-string passer Behren Morton. His path to the roster is hard to see, but it’s only because of all the guys ahead of him. If he continues his strong play, there’s a chance that someone else will pick him up if he ends up on waivers. Running back depth is looking good The Patriots put Terrell Jennings on season-ending injured reserve ahead of Thursday’s game, which means that the RB3 job is now fully up for grabs. Jam Miller, Lan Larison, and newcomers JaMichael Hasty and Hassan Haskins all looked pretty good at times versus Indianapolis. Miller and Haskins are your more bruising backs, and the Patriots do seem to want that, but Larison and Hasty both run hard as well, and are threats in the passing game while also returning kicks. Time will tell who ends up taking that third spot — although my money is on Miller or Larison — but there was no clear winner in the race on Thursday night. The A.J. Brown Bowl awaits With the first preseason game in the books, the Eagles are set to come to town next week for two joint practices, and then obviously the game next Saturday night. I would imagine that those two practices, which happen on Wednesday and Thursday, Aug. 19 and 20, are going to be absolutely jam-packed. It should be a great opportunity for the Patriots to go against a very good team, and see how good this roster really is. And while preseason games are…

title: 5 winners and losers from Patriots’ preseason tie with the Colts
summary: The New England Patriots opened their preseason Thursday night at Gillette Stadium with a 13-13 tie to the Indianapolis Colts. Here is who caught our eye for better or worse upon live-viewing the Patriots’ preseason opener. Winners WR Kyle Williams: The second-year receiver got the Patriots their first preseason touchdown as he showcased his talented […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - AUGUST 13: Kyle Williams #18 of the New England Patriots hauls in a touchdown pass during a game between the New England Patriots and the Indianapolis Colts on August 13, 2026, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Fred Kfoury III/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New England Patriots opened their preseason Thursday night at Gillette Stadium with a 13-13 tie to the Indianapolis Colts . Here is who caught our eye for better or worse upon live-viewing the Patriots’ preseason opener. Winners WR Kyle Williams: The second-year receiver got the Patriots their first preseason touchdown as he showcased his talented release package to win off the line of scrimmage before hauling in a 12-yard back shoulder touchdown from Tommy DeVito. Near the end of the half, Williams then kickstarted a drive by working back through contact and then picking up YAC to record a 25-yard drive starter. The speedster then got open on a downfield go route the very next snap for a potential long score but the ball was under-thrown — although Mike Vrabel shared he would have liked Williams to work back to the ball to try and draw defensive pass interference. Either way, Williams showcased his big-play ability and explosive speed that will earn him a role in this offense. Tommy DeVito. Kyle Williams. Automatic. Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/bVr8miw3qr — NFL (@NFL) August 14, 2026 TE Eli Raridon: The box score shows a measly one catch on four targets for eight yards for the rookie tight end. But, Raridon had a 24-yard reception where he took off out of the flat on a bootleg concept negated due to an illegal man downfield and had a nice block on the Patriots longest run of the night. Raridon was one the wrong side of other plays in the passing game to hurt his box score but his explosiveness and work in the run game passed the eye test. S John Saunders Jr: As he did to end Tuesday’s joint practice, John Saunders recorded an interception off Riley Leonard deep down the middle of the field. The safety, who drew a start next to Dell Pettus and Mike Brown in the secondary, also tallied a pair of run stuffs Losers K Andy Borregales: New England’s sophomore kicker has enjoyed a strong start to training camp of date, but it was a different story as work transitioned to the preseason. Borregales connected on just 2-of-his-5 field goal attempts with misses from 56, 55, and 49 — the final coming with 13 seconds left in a tie game. “We expect him to make them,” Mike Vrabel said . “That’s pro football. They’re banging them in from 60 yards. They have two kickers on their roster. Andy knows we have to make those field goals.” Guard depth: The Patriots guard depth has been a question mark this summer, and that group got off to a poor start both health and performance wise Thursday night. Top interior backup Ben Brown departed with an injury, although the 28-year old shared he was “OK” in the post game locker room as he walked with a limp but no brace, boot, etc. Andrew Rupcich, who has served as the top option next to Brown, also spent time in the blue medical tent but remained on the sideline. Behind them, both James Hudson and Mehki Butler surrendered sacks. Honorable mentions Top rookies: First-round pick Caleb Lomu played 39 snaps at right tackle in his debut. He allowed just one pressure, but was on scene for a run stuff and was downfield to negate Raridon’s explosive. As for Jacas, the pass rusher tallied a run stuff and helped push the pocket on Kindle Vildor’s early interception. Jacas’ aggressiveness worked against him at times, however, as crashed down to allow a 22-yard read option keeper and 17-yard completion in the flat. Before DeVito’s touchdown to Williams, it was a shaky accuracy night for the QB — in addition to backup Behren Morton — with some sprays. Jam Miller was our winner in the RB3 battle tonight carrying the ball 14 times for 55 yards. Lan Larison did post six catches for 38 yards. Efton Chism III had a crisp 20-yard crossing route on third-down on the Patriots first touchdown drive. Kobe Prentice (3 catches, 40 yards) and Cameron Dorner (1 catch, 18 yards) also flashed in the wide receiver room. Bradyn Swinson logged three pressures in 23 pass rush attempts and had a fourth-down batted pass. He did play into the fourth quarter as Jacas and Quintayvious Hutchins drew the start. LB K.J. Britt had back-to-back impact plays with a two-yard TFL before chasing down Anthony Richardson to force a fumble. Rookie cornerback Karon Prunty blew up a perimeter screen by beating his block.

title: Key matchups: Saints vs. Jaguars
summary: The New Orleans Saints finally return to action, hosting the Jacksonville Jaguars in a Preseason Week 1 matchup. Both teams will play with limited starters, as they have a scheduled joint practice on Thursday, with starters getting plenty of playing time then. Despite a lack of starters, there are still plenty of key matchups to […]
full_text: METAIRIE, LOUISIANA - AUGUST 03: Spencer Rattler #2 of the New Orleans Saints and Barion Brown #19 of the New Orleans Saints react during training camp at Ochsner Sports Performance Center on August 03, 2026 in Metairie, Louisiana. (Photo by Morgan Simmons/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints finally return to action, hosting the Jacksonville Jaguars in a Preseason Week 1 matchup. Both teams will play with limited starters, as they have a scheduled joint practice on Thursday, with starters getting plenty of playing time then. Despite a lack of starters, there are still plenty of key matchups to hone in on as the Saints look for their first win of the preseason. Saints pass protection vs. Jaguars pass rush Third-year quarterback Spencer Rattler will be the concentration for Saturday’s matchup. Rattler won the quarterback battle last preseason and has valuable playing time as a starter. Despite going 1-7 as the starter last season, Rattler’s talent and experience should be the difference in the game. Despite this, Rattler has shown a struggle to make plays under pressure, and it will only be emphasized behind the backup offensive line. The offensive line will also be missing Dillon Radunz, who tore his ACL during training camp. Despite injuries and question marks at depth, there are plenty of names to look out for. Jeremiah Wright has the chance to see increased playing time pending his shoulder injury, and Saints fans will get another look at Torricelli Simpkins III, who stood out last season. Offensive line depth has been a struggle for the black and gold in recent years. Facing a young and inexperienced Jaguars pass rush, we will get a close look at how the offensive line reserves look in-game action. Saints wide receivers vs. Jaguars secondary Similar to the offensive line, the Saints have struggled with wide receiver depth in recent seasons. New Orleans has always been one Chris Olave injury away from most teams’ WR5 being their WR1. The Saints addressed them heavily in the 2026 NFL Draft, adding three wide receivers in six rounds. Of these wideouts, fourth-round pick Bryce Lance and sixth-round pick Barrion Brown should see the most playing time. Brown has been one of the best players during training camp, and the preseason will give him the best chance to earn playing time on offense rather than remaining a special teamer, which he was initially drafted for. Jacksonville has some interesting players in the secondary who would likely see playing time. From Tulane’s Caleb Ransaw and cornerback Jarrian Jones, the Jaguars have promising talent waiting for their chance. If Rattler finds any success in the preseason, it will likely be due to a developing connection with the Saints’ young wideouts. Saints secondary vs. Jaguars pass catchers Going into the season, the Saints’ biggest concerns revolved around their young secondary. Highlighted by cornerback Kool-Aid McKinstry, the majority of New Orleans’ projected secondary is on rookie contracts. Even after the addition of Martin Emerson Jr, it appears the Saints are rolling with McKinstry and Quincy Riley as their boundary corners according to the newest depth chart. I’m expecting Riley to get some solid playtime in Saturday’s game alongside Emerson. Jacksonville has a strong trio of wideouts with Brian Thomas Jr, Parker Washington, and Jakobi Meyers, and despite them not expected to play all starters, we’ll likely see atleast of the three. They also have solid depth, with Travis Hunter still listed as a wideout on the depth chart and rookie receiver J0sh Cameron. Saturday should be a good preview of how the Saints’ secondary has developed over the offseason, specifically revolving Riley and Emerson. We may also get a preview of Jonas Sanker in the slot.
author: Kyle Besson

title: Saints vs. Jaguars: Quarterback Matchup
summary: The first preseason game for the New Orleans Saints gets underway this Saturday afternoon, as the Jacksonville Jaguars come to town for the only home preseason game that the Saints will host this season. The game will feature a matchup of Tyler Shough vs. Trevor Lawrence. Now, it’s not known as of today how much […]
full_text: METAIRIE, LOUISIANA - AUGUST 03: Spencer Rattler #2 of the New Orleans Saints and Tyler Shough #6 of the New Orleans Saints participate in a training camp drill at Ochsner Sports Performance Center on August 03, 2026 in Metairie, Louisiana. (Photo by Morgan Simmons/Getty Images) | Getty Images The first preseason game for the New Orleans Saints gets underway this Saturday afternoon, as the Jacksonville Jaguars come to town for the only home preseason game that the Saints will host this season. The game will feature a matchup of Tyler Shough vs. Trevor Lawrence. Now, it’s not known as of today how much either starter will play or if they will play at all. So, with that thought in mind, we will look at both starters and their primary backups. The Saints will also be hosting the Jaguars this week for a joint practice , and those two will definitely be trying to break down the opposing defense. Lawrence is coming off a season that saw the Jaguars finish 13-4, and he had a really solid year himself, finishing the season with just over 4,000 passing yards and completing just under 61% of his attempts. He had 29 touchdowns and 12 interceptions and also added 359 yards on the ground to go along with 9 rushing touchdowns. What was alarming for Lawrence was the number of times he was sacked. He was sacked 41 times in 2025, the sixth-most in the NFL. Lawrence is backed up by veteran journeyman Nick Mullens. He appeared in 5 games last season and attempted only 3 total passes, completing all of them for 19 yards with zero touchdowns and zero interceptions. Over the course of his career, Mullens has a 66% completion percentage but has 34 touchdowns to 31 interceptions in 39 games. Mullens may be getting the bulk of the work on Saturday afternoon for Jacksonville. For the Saints, however, this will most likely be the first preseason start of the 2026 season for Tyler Shough. After having the keys to the franchise turned over to him during the latter part of last season, Shough is looking to come out and build on the success he started having to close out 2025. Shough started the final 9 games, finishing with a 67% completion percentage and just under 2,400 passing yards, 10 touchdowns, and 6 interceptions. He also added 186 yards on the ground along with 3 rushing touchdowns. Shough is exploring this young core of receivers that the front office has added around him, and if he gets the opportunity to start, it will be interesting to see if he can link up with some of the explosive playmakers the Saints have added. The offense has started to find its rhythm as of late in training camp, even though the defense had its number early on. Now, if it’s not Shough starting, then it will be a very familiar face and fan favorite in Spencer Rattler under center for the Saints. It’s hard to think of a better team guy and professional than Rattler. He came into last season as the starter, was replaced midseason, and has taken everything in stride while doing all he can to improve himself and the team. Those results are showing up in camp, as he has been looking pretty good while running with the backup unit. Rattler finished last season with eight starts, 67% completion percentage, just under 1,600 passing yards, 8 touchdowns, and 5 interceptions. Rattler added 167 yards on the ground and 4 fumbles, with 2 of them resulting in turnovers. Either way, this will be a very intriguing matchup of quarterbacks for the first preseason game, no matter who gets the start.

title: Interview with the Enemy: Jacksonville Jaguars
summary: The New Orleans Saints will open the 2026 NFL preseason against the Jacksonville Jaguars at Caesars Superdome on Saturday. To break it down, Gus Logue of Big Cat Country joins us to preview this weekend’s matchup. NJ: With this being the first look at live game action, what are you hoping to learn about the Jaguars that you can’t […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - AUGUST 17: Tyler Shough #6 of the New Orleans Saints is sacked by Travon Walker #44 of the Jacksonville Jaguars during the first quarter of the NFL Preseason 2025 at Caesars Superdome on August 17, 2025 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Sean Gardner/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints will open the 2026 NFL preseason against the Jacksonville Jaguars at Caesars Superdome on Saturday. To break it down, Gus Logue of Big Cat Country joins us to preview this weekend’s matchup. NJ: With this being the first look at live game action, what are you hoping to learn about the Jaguars that you can’t really learn from training camp practices? GL: Head coach Liam Coen has been adamant about two things this offseason: that last year’s run game was the underlying “stink” of Jacksonville’s 8-0 run to cap the regular season, and that it is almost impossible to evaluate the run game without pads. The first day of padded practices at training camp was August 3, so the team hasn’t had many on-field opportunities to improve its rushing efficiency. They’ll also enter this weekend’s matchup with a banged-up O-line and a major question mark at running back. Can the Jaguars’ run game show signs of improvement this early in the football calendar? NJ: Which Jacksonville position battle or group of players do you think has the most to gain from the extra preseason reps against New Orleans? GL: On offense, tight end is a position to watch, as the Jaguars are hoping to get immediate contributions out of rookies Nate Boerkircher and Tanner Koziol. The latter has actually looked more impressive in offseason practices despite being the later pick. Coen will continue to major in 3-WR sets, especially given the depth of the receiver room, but he’d like to be able to lean on 2-TE sets and activate Brenton Strange a little more in the pass game. As for defense, extra preseason reps will be valuable for pass rushers not named Hines-Allen or Walker to prove themselves as worthy depth options. B.J. Green II and Zach Durfee are two young EDGE defenders who have shown encouraging flashes over the past few weeks. NJ: Travis Etienne Jr. left Jacksonville for New Orleans this offseason. How has the Jaguars’ running back room looked without him, and who has stood out as the player most likely to take on a bigger role? GL: This might be the single biggest question for the Jaguars entering the 2026 season. The general expectation is that second-year speedster Bhayshul Tuten will absorb most of Etienne’s workload, free agent pickup Chris Rodriguez Jr. will serve as the between-the-tackles/short-yardage bruiser, and pass pro maestro LeQuint Allen Jr. will see a healthy amount of 3rd down snaps. The backfield may have lost some star power when Etienne left but it is at the very least well-rounded. My personal take is that Rodriguez, who played under Coen at Kentucky in 2021, will be the most trusted player in the backfield and thus earn the bulk of rushing opportunities. But the potential for Tuten to emerge as a star is certainly there. NJ: Who is a Jaguars player you think Saints fans should keep an eye on during Saturday’s game—someone who could make a strong impression despite not receiving much national attention? GL: In Coen’s own words, Jabbar Muhammad is one of the single most improved players on the team compared to this time last year. And we’ve seen it from the sidelines of the practice fields. The former Oregon Duck went undrafted partly due to his size (5′ 9″, 182 lbs), but he is a walking example of the saying, “It’s not the size of the dog in the fight, it’s the size of the fight in the dog.” Muhammad has been all over the ball this offseason, whether in 1-vs-1 drills, 11-vs-11 scrimmages, redzone and two-minute periods, you name it. A strong preseason outing would confirm my belief that he’ll carve out a role on defensive sub-packages by the end of the season. NJ: According to FanDuel Sportsbook , the Saints (-166) are currently 3.5-point favorites over the Jags (+140) in Sunday’s matchup; what is your final score prediction? GL: It’s the first week of the preseason. I think we’re in for a sloppy, turnover-prone, watch-between-your-fingers type of ballgame. Jaguars rookie safety Jalen Huskey’s pick-six won’t be enough in the end; I’ll go Jaguars 13, Saints 17. Thank you again to Gus Logue for joining us to preview this week’s matchup! You can check out the rest of his work here .

title: Our defense vs. their offense: Jacksonville Jaguars
summary: After looking ahead at the New Orleans Saints’ offensive matchup for its preseason opener versus the Jacksonville Jaguars, let’s shift the focus now to the defensive side of the football. With both head coaches announcing there will be little to no action for starters this weekend, it will be crucial to see how the depth […]
full_text: After looking ahead at the New Orleans Saints’ offensive matchup for its preseason opener versus the Jacksonville Jaguars, let’s shift the focus now to the defensive side of the football. With both head coaches announcing there will be little to no action for starters this weekend, it will be crucial to see how the depth of the roster can perform in a real game scenario. Between injuries and the No. 1’s sitting out this game, both coaching staffs will get the chance to see role players, potential starters, and roster bubble athletes hit the field in competition. As many questions linger for New Orleans within their defensive back room, seeing backup players who’ve made plays in practice will be key in truly determining the level they’re currently at. New Saints RB Travis Etienne Jr. last played for Jacksonville so there will no doubt be some familiarity with the opponent in the exhibition contest. While he is unlikely to garner many reps, he could still serve as a factor in working out schemes across the line of scrimmage. Even after finishing last season as a top ten defense in the league, New Orleans lost a couple of veteran leaders in CB Alontae Taylor and LB Demario Davis. This year, the Saints will need to find a voice in the huddle to step up and be a sort of head honcho for the team under Brandon Staley in the defensive coordinator’s second season. As for Jacksonville, they finished 2025 with one of the top offenses in the league. Although starting QB Trevor Lawrence will not be at the helm during this week’s game, Jags’ offensive coordinator Grant Udinski should still put out a formidable gameplan against the black and gold.

title: NY Giants news: Giants set for first preseason game in John Harbaugh Era
summary: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know as the team takes on the Minnesota Vikings in their first preseason game. A Harbaugh team meeting during training camp — an inside look | ESPN.com A Harbaugh team meeting during training camp begins with something he calls “wise words.” This […]
full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know as the team takes on the Minnesota Vikings in their first preseason game. A Harbaugh team meeting during training camp — an inside look | ESPN.com A Harbaugh team meeting during training camp begins with something he calls “wise words.” This is where individual players get up and share a daily message. It’s inspiration or advice, and the order for who speaks is selected based on seniority. Harbaugh used “wise words” throughout his Ravens tenure. Just not always to start meetings. Often, it was after practices. He also employed something called “spotlight” in Baltimore during which a guy would tell his backstory to the team. Veteran wide receiver Odell Beckham Jr. used “wise words” last Tuesday to say: “Yesterday’s touchdown doesn’t win you today’s game.” His point being you can’t rest on the laurels of a good practice. You have to bring it again the following day. Beckham had his second straight strong practice that afternoon. Jaxson Dart is buying into system "I think it's so cool that we have as many coaches as we do that have had head coaching experience, who have done it at such a high level" Jaxson Dart talks about the experience on the Giants' coaching staff: pic.twitter.com/VjfKoYBjdf — SNY Giants (@SNYGiants) August 13, 2026 Odell Beckham Jr.’s quest to make every play count in game that doesn’t | The Record Odell Beckham Jr. is living in two football worlds right now and his current place with the New York Giants has very little to do with his spectacular past. Admittedly, it’s incredibly difficult to separate the two. Which 10 Giants players have the most to gain — and lose — in the preseason opener? | The Athletic C Bryan Hudson. No player has a bigger opportunity than what has been presented to Hudson this week. Starting center John Michael Schmitz has been sidelined since suffering a concussion last Friday. Backup center Lucas Patrick has been sidelined this week while managing a lingering knee injury. With the top two centers on the shelf, Hudson has taken every first-team rep for the past week. That will continue Saturday for Hudson, who impressed in limited action during last year’s preseason. The Giants must have reservations about relying on the 33-year-old Patrick, who has been plagued by injuries throughout his career. The 25-year-old Hudson has a chance to establish himself as the younger, more dependable backup center option. Giants veteran Evan Neal might have shot to make roster after all | New York Post If the 53-man roster is going to include 10 offensive linemen, then the 6-foot-7, 340-pound Neal could steal one of the five backup jobs now that he is listed as a co-second-teamer with Aaron Stinnie at right guard. “I’ve seen great growth from Evan in his ability to take coaching and his ability to try to understand not just how things look on paper but what certain alignments mean to him,” first-year offensive line coach Mike Bloomgren said. “I think he is seeing more in his stance, and he’s playing with more confidence. Listening to other people in the building, they feel like he’s taken some good steps. We’ll see what he’s able to do in these [preseason] games.” Will John Harbaugh trust another rookie kicker after Dominic Zvada’s 62-yard bomb? | New York Daily News Harbaugh knows Zvada’s potential and also his history of inconsistency. That’s why he said: “He does have a big leg, but the bottom line is you got to kick it straight consistently.” And it’s one reason Harbaugh pointed out that lefty Ben Sauls, the other kicker in this competition, “has a very good leg, too.” Zvada clearly has been the better kicker in camp. Most days, with a handful of exceptions, Sauls has missed one or two and Zvada has missed none. Harbaugh and Horton have worked with Zvada on tinkering with the mechanics and operation to help him. The coach so far is splitting time between the two kickers to make it a fair, summer-wide battle. Giants’ fearless rookie insists he can ‘win right now’ if he starts in Week 1 vs. Cowboys | NJ.com Colton Hood is not shying away from his chance to win a starting job. He said he has no doubt he can start in the NFL from the get-go. “Yeah, for sure,” he said. “Like, no question. I know I can…I just know the type of player I am — my technique. My athleticism, I think, is up there with the best of the best. I know I can go out there and compete — and not just compete, but win. So I definitely think I can go out there and win right now.” 1 Player Each NFL Team Should Cut Before the 2026 Season | Bleacher Report New York Giants: WR Jalin Hyatt. Recovering from a torn ACL, wideout Malik Nabers might be ready to play in Week 1. The Giants re-signed Darius Slayton and inked Darnell Mooney and Calvin Austin III to deals in free agency and then drafted Malachi Fields in the third round of the draft. Assuming they all make the roster, Hyatt would be buried on the depth chart. It’s also worth noting that Odell Beckham Jr. has stacked solid performances at training camp in his second stint with the team. He could provide veteran leadership in the receiver room. Hyatt lacks a clear path to a meaningful role in New York and may need a fresh start elsewhere.
